subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, March 25, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide that sums not exceeding $135,000,000 be granted to his majesty for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Vien in the chair.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Last night, just before we went into committee, I had intended to say a few words with respect to this resolution. Yesterday afternoon the leader of the opposition gave an interesting and rather challenging speech upon the subject of Canada's war effort; I should like to refer to one or two of the things he said.
In the first place the hon. gentleman raised the question, "Do the Canadian people realize the gravity of the war situation?" It seems to me that something needs to be said with respect to questions of this kind. It is my opinion that the people of Canada do realize how serious the war situation is, quite as fully as the members of this house do. I know, from my *own personal experience, of hundreds of people who have been trying, ever since war broke out, to find something they could do to help the war effort along. Invariably they have found themselves unable to discover anything they can do. Now I would ask the leader of the opposition this question:	Suppose the
people of Canada did know how serious the war situation was; what could they do? Many of them have no work. What can be done by a man fifty-five years of age, for example, who cannot obtain work in industry, who cannot get the capital with which to go into any kind
of private production and who, if he did go into private production, would be uncertain that he could sell his product at a remunerative price, and even uncertain that he could sell it at all? What can a man in that position do? There are tens of thousands of men in Canada over fifty-five years of age who are eager to do something to help the war along, but who are filled with a sense of frustration because they can find no outlet. If a man is unable to get work it is obvious he cannot contribute any more money than he is already contributing. What can he do? It is important at this time that the minister consider this question, so as to enable people to do more in connection with the war effort.
And now may I ask: What would the position of the leader of the opposition be? Time and again members of the official opposition rise in their places and rail against what is being done, but never once have I heard them offer a suggestion as to how the thing could be done better-not once. I ask the leader of the opposition, not in any spirit of criticism, to tell me what he conceives to be the cause of the deficiency in the war effort-granted that there is a deficiency in the war effort. Does he consider the cause to be a shortage of money? If the cause is a shortage of money, would the leader of the opposition, if he were in power, tax any more rigidly than the Minister of Finance is doing? I would ask the leader of the opposition, too, to tell the committee whether he would borrow any more money than the Minister of Finance is borrowing. And if he could not tax any more or borrow any more than the Minister of Finance is taxing and borrowing, how would he proceed to make Canada's war effort any more effective than it now is? Would he change the system under which we are labouring? The Minister of Finance has not chosen to do that to any great extent, although he is making progressive moves.
The leader of the opposition also spent some time on the question whether we should consider after-the-war conditions. It is my opinion, as one member of the house, that we could scarcely be occupied any more advantageously, either in the house or in the country, than in the discussion of after-the-war conditions. We have no right to assume we are going to lose the war; and even if we had reasonable assurance we were going to lose it we certainly should be prepared for any eventuality which would result from our winning it.
Let us suppose the war lasts six years or ten years, and we persist in trying to manage the affairs of this country in a dive-bomber age by ox-cart methods of finance and
War Appropriation

economy. Under such circumstances what will be the effect upon our war effort? In my judgment it cannot fail to be disastrous. Therefore it would appear to be very important that we discuss some new form of economic system-in the event of our finding such a form-which will enable us to function better. The longer the war lasts the worse will be the dislocation resulting from it, and the greater will be the need for planning now to meet the distressful conditions which are likely to rush upon us as soon as the war is over.
Some people seem to have the idea that every bit of time we spend in planning for after-the-war conditions is of necessity taken away from our work in connection with the war. This is utter nonsense; just as foolish as the assumption that the time we spend in discussions in this house necessarily detracts from our war effort. I believe the Prime Minister has indicated that in his opinion there was no likelihood that the time we would spend in discussing the plebiscite would in any way detract from our war effort. Such discussions are not going to lessen the number of bolts we make, the number of aeroplanes we make, the number of cars, tanks or any other supplies or materials we make. It is not going to lessen the number of men who join up, or the rapidity with which those men learn to fight. How in the world can it mar the war effort?
The time we spend in discussing some new economic system certainly cannot impair the effort with which we wage this war, so far as taking our time or energy or the use of material or money is concerned. I maintain that we certainly should be open and ready to discuss after-the-war conditions so that we may be prepared to go out and meet new situations when they come.
It is my feeling that we must change our order. I am not going to speak in detail on that point. We simply must change the system under which we labour. We must do it, first of all, to get maximum production. We must do it if we are to maintain the health of our people. We must do it if we are to maintain the morale of our people. We must do it if within six or seven years we are to avoid economic or financial collapse. Why not go out and meet these changes before they get to us?
May I draw the attention of hon. members to some conditions which exist to-day under the present system, after more than two years of war. I wish to refer to a passage in an editorial appearing in the Western Producer.

The periodical is commenting on the observations of Mr. Grant Dexter; in the editorial that writer's words are quoted in part. The editorial runs as follows:
But nowhere has Mr. Howe been given authority to organize total war production. The total of our output to-day therefore is the total of orders placed for our own fighting services and for allied governments. Mr. Howe, it appears, has sometimes taken chances.
And then, quoting Mr. Grant Dexter, it
continues:
It is an old story at Ottawa that the general staff hesitate to order more than is needed to meet the immediate requirements. Where the generals or admirals have asked for 100, he, Mr. Howe, has ordered 10,000. But in so doing he has been taking chances and no minister however courageous would go too far out on the limb.
Again, quoting the words of the Western
Producer:
May we ask: What are the general staff and even the minister afraid of? Is it Mr. Ilsley? Is the dead hand of treasury control having the same paralyzing effect here as in Britain?
I am going to ask the minister himself the question asked by the Western Producer: Is this uncertainty, this failure to use our war production capacity to the limit, this failure to do many other things which we ought to do-is this because of Mr. Ilsley? I believe my question has a direct bearing on the appropriation of 8135,000,000 now under consideration, because that is the amount of money to be voted to help pay for what has already been done. The matters we are now discussing are the result of what has already passed. If Mr. Ilsley is the cause of the uncertainty, then it seems to me that fact ought to be made known. And if Mr. Ilsley is in difficulty which he cannot overcome, I say he should take us into his confidence and at least to some extent tell us what his difficulties are, so that we may set about trying to find some way of overcoming them. Otherwise I fail to see how he can possibly be conducting the financial affairs of this country as he ought to be conducting them, in this third year of the war.
I should like now for a moment or two to refer to the Prime Minister's speech made within the last two or three days with respect to the mobilization of man-power. He said things which scare the ordinary person in Canada as regards the way in which he is going to mobilize man-power and woman-power. No one objects to a complete mobilization of man-power and woman-power, but there are many persons in Canada who greatly fear lest some women or some young men shall be

War Appropriation
mobilized and put into their jobs. In order to indicate that what I am saying is not entirely without foundation in fact, may I refer to a statement which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of March 25 under the heading "Mr. M.P." I think I will read this passage. I believe the people of the future would like to know that statements like this did appear in our newspapers as paid advertisements on March 25, 1942, when Canada was supposed to be engaged in an all-out war effort. The statement reads:
Thousands of Autoworkers are Jobless or Facing Unemployment.
What are we going to do about it?
You are assembled now in parliament to bring about the most completely effective allout war effort. Your job is to adopt a programme which will translate the words of Prime Minister Churchill: "Give us the tools and we will finish the job!" into terms that will smash the axis. As Canadian autoworkers we are trying our best to do this job which rests jointly on industry and labour.
But we have found that the job is not being done in the manner which is vital to victory over the axis. In fact, we are so appalled at the mismanagement and continuing blunders in the battle of production that we feel that they must be brought to your attention. We believe that if you are made aware of the facts, you will act as duly elected representatives of the people to see that the deplorable state of affairs existing for many months in the automotive industry is brought to a swift end. Otherwise we face disaster.
Understand-not just remember-Hong Kong and Singapore!
You like all of us, know what happened to Hong Kong and Singapore. We were told that Hong Kong was "well in hand." We were told that Singapore was "well in hand." We are being told that Australia is "well in hand."
But Australia may well go the way of these other bastions of democracy if we do not act quickly. You, Mr. M.P., and the Canadian people must see that it does not happen again. But there is a danger that it can tragically happen unless you learn the truth in time. The truth was hidden from the French people and the republic fell. That should be a lesson to us.
700 G.M. workers have been laid off in Oshawa.
1,500 Chrysler workers will be laid off in W indsor.
2,000 other Ontario automotive workers will be idle.
Idle men and idle machines do not make total war.
Seven hundred skilled autoworkers have been laid off in the General Motors plant at Oshawa and they will be jobless for several months while Australia calls for tools. Thousands of autoworkers in the same plant are working on an average only 30 hours a week producing military trucks which could be used to aid our allies in Russia and other paz-ts of the world when the impending spring offensive begins. Fifteen hundred Chrysler workers and
an estimated two thousand other autoworkers in Ontario face similar lay-offs for several months.
We ask why aren't they working 40, 50, 60 or as many hours weekly as their physical condition permits? We ask why the machines are not working 168 hours weekly producing the tools that Churchill has asked for in the name of the British, Australians, Russians, Chinese and all the peoples of the united nations?
We believe that once you know these facts you will ask the responsible officials of the various departments why these conditions continue to exist, stalling the war effort through idle machines and idle men.
I desist from reading for a minute or two to comment that it has been my impression, gathered from all the information I have gained from men who seem to 'be in a position to know concerning industry all over this dominion, that a condition similar to that here complained of exists everywhere in this country. Now, if a condition similar to what these men depict obtains throughout this dominion, how on earth can we say that we have an all-out war effort? As the Western Producer asks, whose fault is it? Is it the fault of the Minister of Finance? If it is not his fault, then whose is it? I go on with the statement:
Floor show automotive displays do not make total war.
We agree with Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Munitions and Supply, in his public statement last week, that Canada can supply all the military vehicles the united nations can use. We agree that it can be done but it is not being done. Why?
It has been my conviction that Canada could produce all the automotive vehicles that the united nations need. Yet in all probability we lost Hong Kong because of a shortage of such vehicles; with such vehicles we could perhaps have saved Singapore, and if there were in Australia at the present time a sufficient number of tanks and automotive vehicles, I think there would be no anxiety in the hearts of Australians as to their ability to throw off the Japanese attack. Yet the vehicles are not there. They were not in Singapore and they were not in Hong Kong. Here we are in this parliament ready to do anything the Minister of Finance asks, and yet we are unable to get the results we desire. I submit that this is one of the most astonishing situations ever faced by any group of legislators in the history of the world. If the minister had asked us for three billion dollars as a war appropriation, we would have granted it to him just as readily as we shall grant him two billion dollars. If he had asked for six billion dollars, we would have granted it, and it could have been granted. But he has asked for two billion dollars. Last year he asked
War Appropriation

for a certain amount of money and .we granted it to him. All we asked was that he use it in such a way as to bring about a total war effort for Canada. Why is it that we cannot get results in this house? I go on:
We agree with Hon. Humphrey Mitchell, Minister of Labour, that this war will not be won with typewriters.
Neither will it be won with the ftoor show displays in the automotive industry in which men are hastily put on military work on occasions when His Royal Highness, the Duke of Kent, the Governor General or Lieut.-General A. G. L. McNaugbton, commander of the Canadian forces overseas, visit these plants on tours of inspection. We are happy to have them visit our work shops to lend encouragement to the men on the machines but we would rather have them see an all-out war effort than an artificial pretence at one.
There is getting abroad throughout Canada, in every hamlet, in every street and in every tavern, the idea that the fine pictures we see representing Canada's all-out war effort, those fine radio programmes that we hear and which seem .to indicate a feverish degree of activity on the part of the workers, are largely artificial and created to produce a .particular effect. In other .words the Canadian people as a whole are being deceived on a tremendous scale, a scale unprecedented in the history of mankind. I go on:
Who allows such conditions to continue?
It is a shocking picture and we believe you and the Canadian people should be made aware of it. We believe that, knowing the facts, you will act to stop the imperilling of our war effort without any further delay.
We have tried to correct this situation for many months. We have studied the situation thoroughly-and who knows better the existing conditions than autoworkers in these plants?- and made suggestions to no avail. We are still waiting for a conference to discuss this situation with the Department of Munitions and Supply and Mr. J. H. Berry, controller of the automotive industry.
We don't claim to know all there is to know about the problem but we believe it is time that common sense was exercised and industry and labour sat down together to pool their ideas. No one group in the nation is the repository of the brains and brawn that will guarantee a total w'ar effort. They have realized that such conferences are imperative in Great Britain, Australia and the United States if the united nations are to win the war. Who is standing in the way of such labour management conferences in Canada? We have a right to know. You have a right to know.
I think no comment is necessary on that passage. I am going to read another one:
"Let bitterness and discontent get into the hearts of my workers, and, by God, we've lost the war."
That was the statement made by Hon. Ernest Bevin, Britain's Minister of Labour, who is charged with the responsibility of obtaining

maximum production. The same is true of any of the nations where free men are working to drive the nazi menace from the earth. But it is not helpful to their morale to be piddling around at war work. It is not helpful to their morale to be working part time on army trucks when they have been told that every minute, every hour, every day counts.
It is not helpful to their morale after helping to put the victory loan drive over the top to be working short time. It is not helpful to their morale to be thrown on the streets without being eligible for unemployment insurance because they have not worked the maximum 180 days. They want to know what is going to be done about it, Mr. M.P.
I had intended to speak of conditions in Britain, but I find I shall not have time. But I do say that people are going to lose confidence completely in members of parliament. Before I close I wish to refer to what was said by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) the other night, but meanwhile I will finish reading this advertisement. It goes on:
How can members of parliament guarantee total war?
That is the question I ask and every hon. member wants to ask and wants answered. It goes on:
If parliament is to represent the will of the people as it should, you can act to remedy this situation without delay. It is your responsibility to ask those who carry out your will why these conditions we have described only in part continue to exist. You can see that they are stopped. You can see that labour-management conferences are called to end this bottleneck in democracy's arsenal. And we will do our part.

As I said a while ago, this merely indicates a condition prevailing in virtually every industry in the Dominion of Canada, whether it be engaged in producing food, shelter, clothing, or munitions of war. That is a serious statement, but I am positive that if all the facts were brought to light they would establish the truth of what I have said. The mere fact, as the leader of the opposition, I think it was, pointed out yesterday, that we had a national registration in the fall of 1940, which apparently has not so far been used either to determine the extent of our manpower or to put that man-power to work, is I believe one of the greatest condemnations conceivable of this government. And then to think that, without having used the national registration, we should now be contemplating another national registration, and that the Prime Minister should have issued a statement about mobilizing all our man-power

War Appropriation
when he has not taken steps to use the manpower we do know about-the whole thing is so grotesque that it strikes one almost speechless.
I am going to suggest that the government should immediately begin to cooperate with the labouring men; that it should call a round-table council in which the representatives of the men, the representatives of industry and representatives of the government shall get together and make known the actual conditions which exist in any and every industry in the country. I would hesitate to state on the floor of the house at this time some of the things which I have had brought to my attention respecting the conditions of unemployment and inactivity which exist in a good many of our plants. It is such that it simply makes one sick to think of it.
I am going to put once more to the leader of the opposition this question: If he and his party were in power in Canada to-day what would they do to change these conditions?

Then about a year or a year and a half after he had got into power he said in the house that all he had ever intended to do in that respect was exactly what Canada had been doing for the previous twenty years. To regard currency and credit in terms of public need as meaning the amount of credit that people would borrow and the amount of currency that was necessary to back the borrowings is so far away from what currency and credit in terms of public need really means that it is shameful to use the expression to describe the process. Our present system is based on the idea that the money a nation can have is only the amount of money which people will borrow. What the farmers will borrow to raise hogs, what the woollen manufacturers will borrow to manufacture cloth, what the wholesalers will borrow in order to distribute, et cetera-that is supposed to be public need. In an age of plenty, the amount of money which producers will and can borrow for production falls altogether short of public need.
It is right there, in that respect, that the change in monetary management has to take place. The governments and the people who are going to manage the countries of the future must know that money, from this time forward, must be issued not only as debt-money, for production, but also as debt-free money, for consumption. The minute that fact is acknowledged we shall begin to understand how a new order can be set up.
I should like the leader of the opposition to tell us by and by, after he has thought it over, whether he actually thinks that what is physically possible can be also financially oossible. If he actually does, we shall have a Oasis on which to work.
Before I close, I would observe that the amount of money which a nation can have depends on the goods and services, producing and consuming power of the nation, and only on that; and that the money shall be issued not only for production but for consumption, not only as debt money but as debt-free money. Once that is granted, then we shall begin to see how it is that what is physically possible can be made financially possible.
If the Minister of Finance were managing a new system based on that new conception, with the skill, energy and intelligence with which he is administering the present system, he would perform miracles in Canada- miracles of production. He would not have to be offended by advertisements such as the one I have read. He would not have to come here and hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) say that we had gone as far as we possibly could in giving the farmers a

good price, that we have taken every dollar out of the treasury which we can possibly spare. He would realize that the amount we can give to the farmers depends upon our power to produce lumber, coal, butter, milk and cream, fruit and vegetables and other commodities; upon the doctors ready to look after the people, upon the dentists, and others who serve. He would understand that Canada's production of goods and services is what determines the amount which she can pay for wheat and other primary products; not the amount of money the minister can borrow from banks or from any other source, or the amount which he can tax from the people. He would know then how to make what is physically possible financially possible.

The desire has been
expressed by my leader that these bills should pass to-day and I have no intention of holding up their passage, but I want to mention a few matters which hon. members have not had an opportunity of discussing during this session. There are some questions which we have a right to discuss and1 with regard to which we have not been given any information since the war started, of adopting measures for the better protection of the soldiers who serve us overseas or in the three forces, questions such as high cost of living bonus, better pay, national insurance, free railway fares, and leave. In the first place, the House of Commons has completely lost control over expenditures. Where is the auditor general while all this is going on? The last budget which the minister presented was for $1,300,000,000 and now he wants another overdraft of $135,000,000, making for the last year, $1,435,000,000. I have a great deal of sympathy for the minister. He has sat here day in and day out and has devoted himself to his duties and the opposition as a whole has given the government good, independent support. True, there has been criticism, but there has not been enough, our friends back home tell us. The Conservative party secured very nearly half the vote in the last election and we have constituents to represent, and to do our duty and perform our function efficiently as an opposition in a great peril like this war.
Parliament fought for over a hundred years to get control over expenditures in England. There is not one word in the main or other estimates, I would point out to the minister, in regard to matters relating to the war, the price ceiling, grain and so on, and it is difficult to ascertain what the exact state of affairs on our budget for the war really is. I suggest that the public accounts committee should meet and go into these matters. For next year the government is war budgeting for

War Appropriation
$2,200,000,000, which is an increase over last year of about 50 per cent. I do not intend to speak now for more than about fifteen minutes in connection with all these bills, but I suggest that in the recess something should be done to give to the House of Commons that control which it should have over the budget, whether it be in connection with the war or for civilian purposes. Such control is exercised in the old country. There, there is a committee on national expenditures meeting nearly all year, which goes over every dollar of expenditures and every voucher, and coordinates all war effort. We have nothing of that sort. I believe it would be a good thing for us to follow their example. In the British House of Commons certain modern rules are followed which make for expeditious dispatch of business. I support all the rulings of His Honour the respected Speaker, and I support your rulings too, Mr. Chairman. I always pay tribute to the chair and you, sir, also, but I would urge that in the recess the government might take into consideration certain new rules which I shall suggest. I will send copies to the leaders. They can compare the British rules with ours. I think that our standing orders should be amended in accordance with the paragraphs I am going to read.
In a book on parliamentary procedure, 1930, published by G. F. M. Campion, Second Clerk Assistant of the British House Commons-he is now clerk and has been knighted-I read the following:
Not later than three o'clock the question hour begins. This is a more important item of business than any yet described. It is expected to provide lively moments and seems to be of unfailing interest to members and the public. It is modern and affords a useful method of supervising the administration of the government. Its effectiveness is generally recognized. Questions 'turn a searchlight upon every corner of the public service.' (Lowell, i. 332.) Their chief object is 'the explanation to the public of the meaning of political events', and 'they are often arranged by the government itself, so as to give them an opportunity of making announcements in a somewhat informal way.' (Redlieh, ii. 241 and 242). They are 'serviceable as obviating the necessity in many instances of more extended debate and of motions for papers.' (Todd, 1982, ii. 85). And finally, 'Questions afford to the private member under modern conditions almost his only opportunity.' (Marriott, i. 571).
I suggest that our standing order 1, relating to procedure in unprovided cases, should provide that the customs of the British house shall govern. In my opinion, although there is some doubt whether amendment is necessary, this should be considered by the government and by the officers of the house and the three parties.

I wish to speak about two or three other matters relating to the soldier question. We are now at the forty-fifth day of the session. The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Blackmore) said that a debate on the functions of money and the basis of credit is not wasted. He has the right to urge it, but it is a purely domestic question. I contend that the war is primary and should take precedence till it is won. I have been here since the session started, and I have never had an opportunity of mentioning the five or six soldier matters to which I wish to refer but which I will not discuss. As I said last night after 6 o'clock, primary matters should have first consideration in war time and domestic matters wait over. What is the good of talking about changes in our economic system if the war is not won? Life then will not be worth living; there will be no such thing as the price of wheat or the price of anything; everyone will be a slave. We have been here forty-five days and it is almost impossible to get in a few words on behalf of those who are fighting for us. These domestic questions have taken all the time- the plebiscite, the price of wheat, and other local matters.
We are going to have another registry. How many registrations have we had? In 1938, 1939 and 1940 I proposed a national registration of man-power, industrial power, food power and economic power; also a survey of every large and small industry. I urged that about thirty times but it was not adopted. Now we have about six different counts or registers all over again; first the census-and where is all that information to-day? It is not tabulated in such a way as to be of use in the war. Then we had a costly national registration on a huge scale, not worth much so far. My proposal was for a real selective national register two years before the war for security and war and defence purposes, because I saw the war coming and urged this. Now we have another proposed registration of man-power and matters like that by the new Minister of Labour, all over again, which will end in overlapping and doubt and more muddle. I do not believe the new registration to be taken by the Minister of Labour will help our war effort one iota. It is just a duplication and waste of money, because they have all that information already, but it is not tabulated in such a way as to be of use, so a third count is now on in this third war year. Why are all these different people interfering with business and industry and labour so that no man can conduct his own affairs with all these counts so costly and useless? Now they propose to exempt farmers and their sons and help altogether; yet we have never known how many there are available, and we are about the only country in the
War Appropriation

world in which agricultural workers are entirely exempted from military service. How can we win the war when 70 per cent of our population are exempt? In the last war many farmers' sons in Ontario did not vant exemption, and they are not asking for it now. The government has information through those registrations as to the number of farmers' sons who have left the farms and gone to the cities and taken jobs in war and munitions industry, some at $10 or $15 a day with overtime, while the soldiers are fighting for SI .30 a day. Is that fair? Is that the way to beat Hitler? It is not, with these wholesale exemptions of numerous classes. Man-power overseas alone will win the war, not home defence.
This new survey of the Minister of Labour will be a muddle and a sad mistake and a waste of time and will cause endless delays. It is a mistake to exempt farmers. The government have listened to the clamour and agitation of a number of hon. members to do so. There is no scarcity of wheat and grain; in fact there is a large surplus in the world, over 1,500,000,000 bushels, a drug at present on the world's markets. When we have this overproduction why put more men on the land to let them escape military duty? City men are no good on the land. What use would the leader of the opposition or myself or the leader of the house be to-day on the farm? I doubt if we could ride a horse now without falling off. What good would that achieve for farm production or city men as a rule? The thing is ridiculous.
I am asking for better protection for soldiers' dependents, and I ask the two parties to my left for their support. They are asking for $1.41 as a parity price or one dollar for wheat; the soldier is working for $1.30 a day, twenty-four hours a day overseas. Some of them are suffering untold privation on land and sea and in the air and will lose life itself, and they are getting 11 cents a day less than the price asked for a bushel of wheat. I have urged this matter in this house until I am sick of urging it. Some of the ministers, like myself, did not go to the last war. Some of us could not go; I am not here to criticize anyone; I want to be fair, but I was keenly disappointed at the lack of consideration which the Minister of Finance and other hon. gentlemen opposite gave to an application by the soldiers' dependents in this country for a cost-of-living bonus. They have to pay the same prices for groceries and fuel as others do, and I say it was a very hard-hearted answer that was given them by the Minister of Finance. He followed me in the debate on March 4, I think, and replied, opposing

this bonus, that as for paying the poor women at home a cost-of-living bonus, it could not be done. Here we are appropriating these billions of dollars, yet we have not a few cents for the dependents of the soldiers fighting for us and serving overseas. I could take the minister into homes in my own constituency and all over the Toronto district where the dependents cannot live on the pay, with several children, and the soldier's wife has to go out to work or washing in many cases in order to buy a ton of coal or help maintain the home fires. Such a condition is a disgrace, and history will criticize us and condemn this parliament for wasting forty-five days discussing purely domestic questions like a plebiscite and other matters, while conditions of the kind exist. I protest against it. I am sick and tired of it with war matters in the background. We can make no headway here on primary, but only on secondary matters; we might just as well go home, because the executive rules. The executive passed 26,000 orders in council, and goodness knows what the deficits will be next year when we have such a huge one for the end of this year, March 31.
I stood in front of the Chateau Laurier the other day and watched able-bodied uniformed men in the pay of the government, some officers in cars, some of whom have never been in this war or the last, and they have able-bodied young soldiers driving them round the city.
Another question I have raised is with regard to a national system of soldiers' insurance. On every soldier the cost would be little. No reply has been given concerning that. If you ask the government about it they simply say that it is a matter of policy and that any announcement will be made in due course. We have been told that three or four times, the past two years in succession.
The question has been raised of free transportation for soldiers. I travel in only one province, though before I was a member at one time I travelled quite a bit. But when I see some of the luxurious cars occupied by those engaged in sports and for conventions and theatre and Hollywood1 people, and then see the cars occupied by the soldiers who are going over to fight this war for us, I protest, and I ask for a change by the railways and better accommodation for the aid parliament gives them. I do not think the present system in regard to soldiers' fares and meals on trains is fair. Here we are asked to vote a postmortem, as it were, because we cannot strike off one cent of the $135 million or the other votes.
Another question is the housing problem. In 1934 and 1935 the construction trade was

War Appropriation
almost down and out. In January, 1935, I moved for a committee on housing. One was appointed a little later on, and on the basis of the report of that committee the new and present government, in 1936 and 1937, did good work, bringing about the spending of some $72,000,000 to date in connection with small housing construction. May 1 is almost here again; civilians and soldiers alike are being turned out of their houses, and I would ask that the old housing administration's policy of the last four years be continued at least until a year after the war.
Some time ago, just after the present Minister of National Defence took office, I offered a suggestion which I want to renew to-d'ay. I greatly sympathize with anyone who has to carry in that department the burdens of government in these war days; but I believe in British Columbia, in the maritimes, in the St. Lawrence ports and elsewhere, in cooperation with school boards, provinces and municipalities, an attempt should be made to teach every man, woman and child to handle a rifle. That was done in Norway and1 Finland, and those people put up a great home battle. British Columbia will not be able to do so well, I am afraid. In Finland and Norway they had miniature ranges, where the people were taught to shoot, and as a result great numbers of invading Germans were destroyed. It is true that we have no army rifles to spare at the moment, but we could provide miniature rifles and ranges and give instruction to all the people in these vulnerable named1 areas.
Before the Easter adjournment I think the government would be well advised to give us further information with regard to shipping losses in the Atlantic. I am only going to mention the matter; I do not want to discuss it. The losses in men and tonnage have been appalling from the lack of bases in Eire. We are at times losing more ships than we are able to turn out. Shipping should have first priority, not only in Canada but in all the united allied nations, and I think something should be done in this connection. The same thing applies in the Pacific. I am sorry we cannot give more help to Australia, and I cannot help feeling that in some ways we did not do our duty toward that country before war started or at the imperial conference of 1937 and after it. We should have joined in an empire shipbuilding policy, such as was proposed in 1937, a grant to the Singapore base and adopted the Jellicoe report. I give the government credit; they have done well in many ways, but my point is that we have done only about one-third of what we should do and we have not yet done enough for a total war effort. I believe also that we should recognize General de Gaulle, who has taken action in
the approaches to the St. Lawrence at St. Pierre and Miquelon, to keep enemy submarines, lurking there to destroy our ships, away from our cargo and troop ships. Then I would abolish the censorship of the press; and, if the Minister of Labour is going to take over the duties in regard to industry which were announced the other day, there would be no further necessity for the Department of National War Services. It would only be duplication; the unemployment insurance department and the three war departments could do some of it.
I disagree with the theory that the farm is our first line of defence. The first line of defence of Canada in man-power, and our only defence, is overseas; and if that falls all our home defence will not amount to anything. The defence of Canada is not and1 will not be decided in Vancouver, Halifax, Saint John, Quebec or Montreal; it is being decided overseas and in the battle of the Atlantic, the Pacific, Africa and the far east; and if that line of defence fails, the enemy will be here in Canada in no time and home defence will not amount to much. Why, even if we had a million men we could not do anything in the Pacific, as Mr. Churchill has said, because Japan has command of the whole Pacific ocean, north and south, and her ships can roam like a circus wherever they please, for 15.000 miles among the Pacific islands. How can we stop her? We were offered three or four destroyers and cruisers by the British government in 1937 and urged by Jellicoe to get more, but because of our pacifist sentiments we did not accept the offer to rearm before it was too late, since we depended solely on America's aid in the Pacific.
I think it was a mistake for Admiral Jones and Canada's navy heads, to make the statement they did make in this city to press men the day before yesterday. As head of an important branch of our naval service, that so-called silent arm of the services, he summoned the press and gave them an interview. Surely that is not in the tradition of the silent service. I believe it was a mistake to make that information available to Japan and Germany, who have their agents all over Canada and know our plans. Such talk will hurt us. This incident reminds me of the situation which arose between the two admirals in Halifax not long ago. Under the statute of Westminster the British fleet cannot come closer to our shores than the three-mile limit; they cannot get into Halifax or Victoria, and I think that is one of the greatest mistakes we ever made, because we owe our protection to the British fleet. I predicted in 1937 and 1938, if war came, we faced the possibility of the invasion of the St. Lawrence then.
War Appropriation

I should like to refer to what is going on in connection with competitive industry in this country. It will be noticed that the amount covered by this resolution has to do with a number of civilian departments which apparently had overdrawn their appropriation in the $135 million. A list of these departments is shown at page 1556 of Hansard, in the breakdown given there, and among them is the Department of External Affairs. Before the war we spent a great deal of money through this department to establish high commissioners and legations all over the world, and I think that was another great mistake because it divided Britain's representation status. We had at our disposal our representatives in these places, our trade commissioners, and! it was a most mischievous policy to follow, fatal in war and of little value in peace. The war has cleared some of them up.
In conclusion, may I say that "never were there so many who knew so little about so much"; and I am referring to the speech by Mr. Gordon in which he told the people of Canada, on behalf of the government, what they should expect and the abolition of all competitive business. All these announcements in the newspapers and speeches over the radio show that Mr. Gordon is acting as a sounding board for the government. Why, even the House of Commons has not been consulted about these changes in our economic system although in session, nor told a thing about it. Our friends to my left have been talking about our economic system and our domestic matters for forty-six days this session, but it was the old competitive system that built up this country in the days of Macdonald and Laurier when everyone owned a small property. It was that system of thrift, with the right fundamentally to possess private property, that made this country and the dominions rich and prosperous. That is the fundamental basis and principle of all sound finance and commerce the empire over. I am not one of those who want to live in the past. I want to rewrite it to meet modern conditions and bring it up to date, because we are entering upon a new world. I have always been a friend of labour consistently, but I would say that the right to possess private property is derived from nature, not from man, and the state has no right to abolish it, but only to regulate its use.
People are wondering what this House of Commons is for, and what minister of the crown is responsible to parliament for all the ins and outs of this wartime prices and trade board and all their controllers and legion of officials. Is all competitive industry to die and wither away, as Mr. Gordon says, over our heads? Is

everybody to become an employee of the government, under national ownership, with every worker on a farm to receive $15 a week? The small business man might just as well close up and go out of business; the retail trade of Toronto might just as well quit because no independent private business man can function and make a living. I do not believe in that system, with all the artificial barriers, burdens and restraints put on him. At the beginning of the war, and up to 1941 the old policy was maintained, "no commitments; parliament will decide," but now that has gone to the archives, following all the announcements that have been made by these various people, and bureaucratic czars over the head of parliament. The public will agree to any regulation so long as they know it is helping the war effort, but a great many of these things have no relation to the war at all. In those cases we should have something to say, I believe.
I am free to admit that so far as such necessities of life as food, clothing, fuel and many other domestic things are concerned, some regulation may be quite necessary, and the public will agree to it if necessary and are glad to comply for the sake of the war. But that is not the case in connection with many other commodities, and the rationalization and streamlining, zoning policy made nationally in everything, with bonuses and subsidies as well will lead to untold abuses and no one knows at what cost.
No doubt war production should have priority, but there are very few walks of life to-day which are not supervised or directed by some department of state at Ottawa. Canada is fighting this war with Britain as her leader for two real objects- to keep Britain, the dominions and our allies free, and to see that Canada and Britain may enjoy prosperity. If Germany were to win we would lose our freedom; they would grind us as slaves to the earth. If Germany wins, still more bureaucrats wall be here, and our freedom will wither away and life will not be worth living. This new belated plan of controlling everything, this heterogeneous device with respect to man-power threatens our economic and commercial and trade freedom. It will not half of it, help the winning of the war or help one iota to beat Hitler, or assist in bringing about a total war effort It will only cause, like the new registration, more muddle, confusion, waste, duplication of services, coma, doubt, inertia, vacuum and expense, and in the end national bankruptcy. There will no doubt be a complicated duplication and multiplication

War Appropriation
of numerous new boards to ruin retail and small business and our industries, and in the end cause unemployment.
The new plan of exemptions eliminates about 70 per cent of the population from military service altogether. It will lead to a muddle in man-power, hurt our army, navy and air force, and cause confusion in trade and industry. Industry does not yet know what it is or where it will lead to. Is the war policy of the government to be that the government is to control and administer every walk of life and almost every article or commodity of trade and commerce, and all competitive business? If so, it will lead this country to disaster and, in my opinion, sooner or later, national bankruptcy. It will not help the war effort and they will try to continue it after the war on international grounds. In England an act has been passed to restore former trade practices as before the war. One should be passed here.
New departments are being created all along the line. May I point out, too, that I am sick and tired of all these orders in council by officials and registrars in the making, who have never had to deal in business with masses of men, or to shoulder any responsibility, or even to take any risks or serve in a competitive calling, but are merely theorists. They tell us of brave new worlds to conquer and to come; and if we were to follow them we would invite and bring nearer in Canada decay, ruin, stagnation, economic slavery, ruined enterprises both large and small, closed factories, and no work for our people. It will all end in doom for all competitive business, with a mighty host and a large standing army of inspectors, examiners, dreamers, supervisors and registrars, regulators, clerks, stenographers, cardfiling officials and stamp clerks. It would be a mere nepotist army, also, the way these boards have selected all their people. Many of these new departments have more than one of the same family on their payrolls. The fact that we are at war and are in desperate need is no good reason why some of these matters should be adopted but not be discussed. We should be less ready, as a House of Commons, to tolerate any method which is not meant to win the war. When we know that seventy-five per cent of them do not help at all in winning the war, then we ought to object to them, and insist that when parliament is meeting this is the place to announce them.
The system which has been introduced supplants courageous leadership and courageous business men, most of whom by a small
start got a good small or large business together. But these new departments by dilatory methods and aim are going round in a circle, and the adoption of cumbersome routine, will fundamentally destroy Canada in time and not help win the war. It is likely, however, that the new condition will want to continue in business after the war is over. Those new boards are going to find some excuse to continue after the war, but in England they are checked by the act passed to restore pre-war trade practices to aid trade.
For three or four centuries Britain has proved that free men and free enterprise would lead, the world over, and this made her not only the mart of all the world but the leader in trade and commerce. Now we are asked by dreamers, theorists and officials to surrender it all; we are asked to Surrender it for new plans and new schemes impossible of fulfilment. I can say to the minister and to some of his deputies that a good deal of this has been introduced by theorists who never had any dealings in any Canadian competitive business. They were imbued with new-found, socialist ideas, or whatever they were. They do not understand cause and effect of those theories on retail and wholesale business or on any business, and will hurt labour and its best national interests. It is a design which will ruin our system which made British and empire trade. The press and members of parliament to-day have come to the point where they should do something to combat this condition and insist on parliamentary control over it or a discussion here. I will admit that much has been done by some of these boards to keep down some well-needed prices. That procedure may have been all right. But to put a ceiling over all prices by subsidies for some, not others, and to abolish competition, something upon which the two older political parties have based their whole history, and upon which the economic trade and commercial history of this country is based, and to destroy it over our heads is not a proper procedure. The older parties in Canada have always encouraged private independent business; surely they would be sorry to see it go. If it passes away, then I say we shall be in just as bad a position as Germany-a nation run by bureaucrats, something we are fighting in this war for freedom of everything and to make our country have proper security for its people and work for our people under a new deal worth living for; for everyone.

I did withdraw it. As I was saying when this other matter arose, the coal industry is in need of more efficient planning. It must look strange to the Canadian people to see the government subsidizing imported coal while our own mines are idle. I am going to mention a number of matters at this time because the Minister of Finance is in the chamber. While these matters may refer particularly to the Department of Pensions and National Health and the Department of Munitions and Supply, they involve additional expenditure and therefore must be approved by the treasury board.

War Appropriation
I would call the attention of the minister to the basic training being given cadets in our schools. These are our future soldiers. Under the present system there is a duplication of work and a waste of time and money. Cadets are trained for the three services, the navy, the army and the air force. The initial or basic training consists of some two hundred hours, and it is the same for all forces. But at present the different cadets are being handled separately, which necessitates more instructors. One instructor could do the work now being done by three. Then the matter of uniform comes into question. The most attractive uniform attracts the most cadets; they all want to get into the air force. This is the problem created for those who are handling the cadets. The boys in our high schools who are taking this basic training will be the soldiers of to-morrow. If they get this training under proper supervision the need for it on the parade ground will be largely eliminated. In addition they receive sixteen hours of specialized training to fit them for whatever unit they may want to join after leaving the cadet corps. This is all very useful work, but an analysis should be made in order to eliminate any defects that might exist.
Another matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention is in connection with the air force cadets. This corps is organized on a charitable basis. The work is necessary and could be productive of much good. At the present time committees in the different communities are obliged to raise money by appeals to public-spirited citizens and the work is financed in this way. Teachers who receive honorary appointments as officers in the corps are obliged to buy their own uniforms and so forth. Many of them cannot afford to do this. They would like to do something but they are placed in an awkward position because they cannot afford this expenditure. I think money should be appropriated for this purpose and the work should be directed by the Department of National Defence. I call this to the attention of the minister because if any change is proposed the matter will be brought before the treasury board which will say whether or not an expenditure is justified.
I have received a number of complaints from men in the armed forces who are desirous of adopting children. If a child is adopted subsequent to enlistment, as the regulations now stand no pay and allowances can be granted. Many institutions across Canada are trying to find homes for unfortunate children and their work is carried on on a charitable basis. Many men in the armed forces have
adopted children but they cannot get any allowance, and more would1 adopt them if allowances were available. The present regulations are retarding a necessary endeavour and depriving children of homes. Many persons who would like to have children in their homes are blocked by the regulations. I mention this so the minister may give it some consideration.
I think the gasoline regulations discriminate against clergymen. Drugless healers and others are permitted a mileage of 15,000, but clergymen get only half this amount. In the community from which I come the clergyman is as necessary as the doctor. He has many calls to make at all hours of the day; he covers a large territory; he is on call day and night. Some consideration should be given to him. At least our regulations should conform to those in the United States; clergymen in Canada should receive the same consideration as is given to clergymen in that country.
I should like to say a word or two about wartime housing. Before coming to Ottawa for this session the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and I met the city council of Sydney. There is a serious housing shortage in that city. Perhaps 1,000 more men are employed in the steel plant to-day than were employed prior to the war. A plate mill has recently been opened which will employ from 400 to 600 men. During the summer months hundreds of men come in and out of this port. An air field has been established there and this has brought another group of men to the city. The officials are at their wit's end to provide wartime housing. They told us that their requirements are at least 500 additional houses. I understand a report was made to the government. The city council urged that we tiy to do something about this, that we bring it to the attention of the government for consideration.
Another matter about which I have corresponded with the government has to do with the facilities for shipping at this port. Perhaps 2,000 ships used this port last year and there are no wharfage facilities available. If a ship comes in slightly damaged there is no way to get its cargo out. Those who are endeavouring to regulate traffic in and out of the port have a serious problem on their hands. I urge that some consideration be given to providing facilities for commercial shipping. This is not for naval purposes; it is for the purpose of taking care of the growing flood' of traffic in and out of this port occasioned by the war.

War Appropriation

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the plight of the retail gasoline dealer. We all realize that the use of gasoline for domestic purposes should be reduced as much as possible, but if the regulations are effective it will mean that many retail gasoline dealers will be put out of business. The more effective the regulations are, the greater the number of retail gasoline dealers who will be put out of business. Many of them have an investment in this business; a good many of them run a repair shop in connection with the station, but gasoline is the main attraction. Their costs have gone up from 20 to 30 per cent since the outbreak of war, and now that they are being legislated completely out of business they at least have the right to know whether the government can utilize their plants. If not, some compensation should be granted to them for the loss they are sustaining. The government is practically taking over their business of selling gasoline, and the retail gasoline dealers should be compensated on the basis of replacement value. I suggest that that question be given consideration. The regulations are unjust to the average retail dealer because in addition to all the restrictions put upon his business the oil controller has permitted wholesalers, for example, who were purchasing 500 gallons of gasoline a week from the local dealers to put in their own tanks. Owners of commercial vehicles can also put in their own tanks. The retail dealer is being legislated out of the picture. He is being treated unjustly in comparison with the big oil companies which have been getting a two-cent increase on their sales since the outbreak of war, while the retail dealer got absolutely nothing. His business has shrunk about 50 per cent, while his costs have gone up. He is liable for cost-of-living bonus, must pay increased costs in other directions due to the war, and is receiving no consideration. I rise for the purpose of bringing this to the attention of the Minister of Finance, because in the final analysis all these things must pass through the treasury board.
I suggest also that the Minister of Pensions and National Health give consideration to extending the allowance to adopted children so that children who have been adopted subsequent to the soldier's enlistment can be taken care of. The regulations do not cover that now.
1 am sorry, Mr. Chairman, to have taken up the time of the committee, and I would not have done so had you received the cooperation of the committee in the manner suggested by the minister.

speechtext:
May I say to the
Minister of National Defence in regard to the money to be appropriated under this resolution that many people both in the house and outside have suggested that a rehabilitation fund be set up for the armed forces which would be available for their use after the war. I realize that there may be reasons, although they are not very clear to me, why the armed forces should not be receiving higher pay at the moment. But I suggest in all sincerity that nothing could do more to improve the morale of the men in the armed forces of Canada than for the government to set aside a savings fund, a rehabilitation fund, if you will, in which the armed forces would have a real stake after their fighting days are over. I have always been strongly in favour of such a fund. I think one other member has already drawn it to the attention of the house. It seems to
me that in our national selective service arrangements we are faced with two problems which are very difficult of solution. First we are up against the lack of parity-we have used the word parity in many debates on agriculture, and lack of parity seems to me to present one of the greatest difficulties in connection with national selective service, as I think the minister will agree. Here you have on the one side, agriculture, which is a wartime industry, and as the months go by I feel that agriculture will be recognized as an essential wartime industry even more than it has ever been before. I am not going to make a special plea on behalf of the farmer to-day except to mention that the farmer is definitely operating under a lack of parity of return as compared with other wartime industries.
In addition to that, the armed forces are working under a similar disability. If we are to put into effect a definite national war-time selective service in Canada, it behooves the government and parliament, from the point of view of financial and economic returns, to treat our farmers and the men in the armed forces on a basis of equality of remuneration with other war-time activities. I hope that the committee and the ministers in charge will take into serious consideration the question of setting aside for our soldiers, airmen and sailors some kind of rehabilitation fund so that in addition to the pay they receive, and the allowances they are given by virtue of service in the forces, they will have each month or year, as the case may be, set aside for them, something in the way of a savings fund in order that they may have a substantial stake at the end of the war. That is important in the interests of morale at the present time and of the welfare of the men at the close of the war. The men, I think, will find it easier to rehabilitate themselves and to resume their normal places in our civilian life if they are given something to start with instead of coming back not fully provided for. I make that suggestion seriously. I think it is one of the most important points which the government can deal with at the moment, and I couple with it the question of agriculture which I brought up a moment ago.

are fully aware of the steps which have been taken, and they are certainly steps in the right direction. My main objection is that they do not go far enough. They do not provide a really large enough fund against the time when the men are discharged, because one cannot do much with one month's pay and with a few odds and ends of that sort. I should like to see the men in our armed forces come back to their normal activities in Canada without being penalized financially or economically by reason of the fact that they have served overseas or in Canada in the forces.

discrepancy when one speaks of $1.30 a day and compares that with wages paid in industry, but there are more compensating factors to be taken into consideration. Might I turn from that to a very plebian subject, the ten million pairs of socks. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I wish to make two brief observations. The first relates to a number of letters I am receiving from people who use cars in their business and who are not classified
for gasoline rations in a class that permits them to continue in business. I will describe one instance that is more or less typical.
I know a man who deals in automotive supplies and travels from garage to garage all over western Ontario. He bought a big old-fashioned car and uses it as a truck with shelves in the back seat to carry his goods. He writes telling me that he will be forced to give up his business, in which he has been engaged for some twenty years, because the amount of gasoline allowed him is not sufficient to enable him to carry on. I know the government do not want to drive small business men out of business; the Minister of Finance needs the revenue. If thousands of small business men like the one I mention are forced out of business, that will be detrimental to the revenue. I think the differentiation between a car such as this used in business, practically a truck, and a private car, should be looked into very carefully.
Another matter about which I am greatly concerned is the direction of the road from south of the Peace river to connect with the Alaska highway at Fort St. John. I have been in that area; I am not perhaps as familiar with it as those who live there, but I made a careful survey by photograph and otherwise and I think I know the situation. I know that the government wants to do what it can to expedite travel north of the Peace river in the direction of the Alaska highway. My observation was that that country might possibly be invaded. There is a great deal of prairie; the mountains are not so wide at the north end of British Columbia; and while I hope no invasion takes place, it is imperative that this country be in a position to transport numbers of troops rapidly to defend1 it against invasion. The other day we had a statement tabled here, not of the direction the road is to take from Edmonton to Fort St. John, but of several directions that it could take. In my opinion every consideration but speed should be disregarded as far as the direction the road should take in war time is concerned.
It is some 267 miles from Edmonton by rail to the railway junction point south of the river at McLennan. There the railway branches, one branch going directly north or northwest and crossing the Peace river at the town of Peace River, some fifty miles northwest of McLennan. This branch of the railway then continues west on the north side of the Peace river for some sixty-four miles to Hines Creek. That is the terminus on the north side of the river. Last fall-hon. members from Alberta will be able to tell the time better than I-the Alberta government, very rightly in my
War Appropriation

opinion, subscribed money to project the highway west of Hines Creek in the direction of the British Columbia boundary. The British Columbia government-and the British Columbia members will know better than I, particularly the hon. member for Cariboo-projected their highway eastward towards the Alberta border with the intention that the two highways would meet. That road is constructed to a considerable extent. On the north side of the Peace, one river has to be bridged, not a large river as we consider rivers here, and very small in comparison with the Peace river. Both in northern British Columbia and northern Alberta, they have been working to have that road completed. It is not completed. I am convinced that this government should advance whatever is required to complete, as an essential military project, that highway from Hines Creek to Rose Prairie, which is some twelve miles north of Port St. John, because the only bridge over the Peace river is that at the town of Peace River. That is a huge bridge, longer I think than this across the Ottawa river here. I believe it is something around 1,800 feet or more in length. Why there is any delay in completing the road west of Hines Creek I cannot understand. In my judgment its completion is absolutely imperative as a military necessity.
There is another roadway, as the Prime Minister pointed out, a much longer one, running west of McLennan to Rycroft, where it turns immediately to the left and runs away to the south approximately fifty miles, then northwest to Dawson Creek. When it reaches Dawson Creek it is a matter of fifty miles more or less to Port St. John, but between those two points this huge river has to be crossed by ferry, and shortly, when the ice breaks and the spring freshets come, it will be some time before a boat could cross that river. Once the ice is gone and the floes have disappeared, they could cross on a pontoon bridge, if one were constructed. There is not one there now, or rather there has not been one up to the present time. So, from the point of view of a military project the government should waste no further time in attempting to develop the roadway, and I believe also the railway, west from its terminus at Hines Creek to Rose Prairie, which will be on the road from Fort St. John to Alaska.
I appreciate tlhe opportunity of making these few observations, because I am interested in these two matters and particularly, if I may say so, in the defence of that vast country in the Pacific northwest, and our ability to get to it rapidly in case that defence becomes necessary.

speechtext:
I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Defence one matter based on sessional paper No. 154. In a committee where we seem to be talking all the time in terms of millions and billions, it may seem picayune to bring up a matter concerning only several thousand dollars, but I should like to point out that the average .man on the street, particularly in a small community, does not deal with millions of dollars. He deals with the few thousand dollars spent in his locality, and he forms his impression as to how we are administering public funds from what he sees in his immediate vicinity. Personally I always feel sad when what seems like a glaring example of poor management tends to destroy the public confidence of a coimmunity, especially a com-munty such as the one from .which I come, where enlistments have been high and support for the war has been very strong.
I am referring now to the Weyburn barracks. I am not going to take time to do more than point out the highlights of the matter to the minister. The first battalion of the South Saskatchewan regiment, stationed at Weyburn, was mobilized immediately on the outbreak of war. In order to secure a barracks the government rented the International Harvester building, -which was a very good building, and spent some $7,229.65 in equipping it; paid $560 a month rent; kept it in repair from time to time, spending on one occasion $1,773.72 and on another $1,196.94 for repairs. The building gave excellent service. The first battalion of the South Saskatchewan regiment trained there -until a few months before it left for overseas, and another regiment also trained there. The barracks was closed for a time, and then the second battalion of the South Saskatchewan regiment was stationed' there for training.
Last fall some officer was sent into the district, and he intimated that the government were not prepared to continue -paying $560 a month rent for a -barracks which was used only fro-m time to time, and that it was -intended to close, the barracks. My information, from those imho are in a position to know, is that the general manager of the International Harvester company put it up to the government in this way. He said, "We do not expect you to pay this rent. We are prepared to let you leave your equipment there; let the building stand as it is and we will charge nothing at all, even for the storage of the equipment. We are not likely to use the building in these

War Appropriation
times, and when you want it again you can take it over." The reply of the officer was, "Well, those are not my orders. We must proceed to take out all the equipment and fixtures we put in, and place the building back in the shape in which we found it in 1939." That was done, at a cost of some $1,840.70, with the result that the building is now back in the shape in which it was before and is not available as a barracks should the occasion arise to use it as such. In all, we have spent on that building $39,209.82.

Yes, including maintenance, repairs and rent, and of course I point out that a large part of that total is rent, amounting to $14,560; but that still leaves $25,000 which has been spent on maintenance and repair. I am not objecting to that at all. What I am pointing out is that here was one of the finest barracks in western Canada. It is not just a matter of closing it; it is a matter of spending nearly $2,000 to take out all the fixtures, which in all probability will have to be put back again. Should certain contingencies materialize on either coast; should the second battalion of the South Saskatchewan regiment have to be mobilized, that barracks will have to be used again, because it is the only place available. We are talking about building training centres for the trainees. Here was one of the finest barracks, capable of accommodating anywhere from eight hundred to a thousand men.
I ask the committee to consider the impression on the public mind. Here is a barracks on which we, the public, have spent money. Perhaps there is no need to use it at the moment; but why spend $2,000 to take out plumbing fixtures, heating equipment, equipment for showers and so on, and probably have to spend several thousand dollars more putting them all back some time later? It seems to me this was a case of red tape actually interfering in what would have been an ordinary, common sense business transaction of accepting the offer of the International Harvester company to let the building stand idle, to waive the rent and storage charges, so that in the event of the building being required the arrangement could have been picked up again right where it was dropped.

I wish to congratulate the Minister of National Defence upon his statement that there was no service which ranked as high as that of the man who offered his life for his country. I think we are quite in agreement with that, but I do not believe that is sufficient. It is all right to offer platitudes and praise to the men of the fighting forces, but I think that must be supplemented- with something a little more concrete. I do not think anything would please the soldiers more than to be given a little better financial consideration.
That recalls to my mind a question which I have brought to the attention of the Minister of National Defence since war broke out; that is, the matter of the treatment given those in the army, as compared with the treatment given those in the other services. I recall when I left to come to Ottawa for this session, standing in the station at Calgary and seeing a colonial train pull out ahead of us. There were quite a number of soldiers standing there, and when that colonial train had pulled out of the station I went to the policeman at the door and asked whether the soldiers were going on that train. He said they were. I said, "Well, that seems queer. What is the matter with these air force fellows, and these navy men? Do they not go on the same train?" His reply was, "No, none of them are going on that train." I thought what a tragic situation that was, that because some of those men happened to be in the army they were packed off on a colonial train, while others, members of the air force and the navy

and I am not complaining about their treatment-were allowed to go tourist. I do not think that is conducive to good feeling.

from the standards with which officers are accommodated-the very best of accommodation-and on through to the tourist class, where the air force and the navy received excellent accommodation.
