subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is another point I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. One of the greatest problems with which we are faced is that of production. Of all the things which will contribute most to our war effort, certainly production stands at the top. In the last couple of years we have seen what happens when our forces are not properly equipped. There is absolutely no question about it that we are not producing anywhere near what we should be producing. I have no doubt all hon. members received a copy of the Financial Post this morning. In that issue it is stated that we are turning out about 25 per cent to 30 per cent of the amount of production we could turn out. Not long ago the Prime Minister said that we are turning out about 44 per cent. I believe the figure of 30 per cent gives a fair estimate of our production at the present time. It is not good for the morale of our people to see manufacturing industries which are idle. We have an illustration right here in Ottawa, one which has not yet been corrected. I refer to the laying off of 500 men by the Ottawa Car and Aircraft. To my mind that is next to criminal. There is another situation in Oshawa where it has been estimated that 700 men have been laid off. Another 1,500 men are going to be laid off by the Chrysler works. Another 2,000 are to be laid off in other automotive industries. There is no question in the world that such a condition should not prevail.
I was interested in the meeting called the other day and attended by automotive workers who came from Oshawa and Windsor to interview ministers in the government. I believe they spoke to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the Minister of Labour. Those men suggested that the ministers should go into the streets of Oshawa and Windsor, and listen to the comments made by the workmen, and by people generally. I hear those comments every time I come to Ottawa on the train, and I do not believe I would be exaggerating if I were to say that the people of Canada are fast reaching the belief that there is no concerted war effort, and that the government has no definitely laid plan.
The men who came to Ottawa the other day were as sincere a group of workers as one would find anywhere. Their desire was not that of embarrassing the government, but rather to assist labour and industry to organize so as to bring about greater production. That was their only purpose, and surely it was a most commendable procedure for those men, who came here at their own expense.

War Appropriation
I was particularly interested in the condition in regard to tool and die-making in Oshawa. It is my understanding that one of the greatest lags in industry is caused through lack of proper dies and/ tooling equipment. The General Motors plant has laid off over 700 workers, and the excuse given by the minister is that the men were laid off because the plant was tooling up for a new order. But while that was taking place, a considerable number of experienced tool and die-makers were out of work in Oshawa. I understand a small fraction of those men were working full time, and some were receiving overtime. Others were working only five or six hours a day. To my mind that condition suggests a lack of coordination and organization. I believe the men /who came to Ottawa the other day left with the government a very good suggestion. Whether it will be worked upon, remains to be seen.
They pointed out that one of the great difficulties in production centred round the speedy production of dies and tools, and they made the suggestion that tool and die workers should be organized into a pool. This pool would be supervised by the government, by the workers through their trade unions, and by industry. The result would be that when there was a job of tooling up and die-making for certain contracts, the government could keep those tool and die-makers busy all the time. Under proper supervision and organization blueprints could be sent to those men, and from those blueprints, even if it were necessary to work twenty-four hours a day, the required tools and dies could be made.
I cannot understand why the government does not awaken more readily to the seriousness of the situation. One of the ministers has pointed out that one of the greatest difficulties has -been the production of tools and dies, thereby causing a lay-off of from 700 to 1,500 to 2,000 men. That is a tremendous waste of man-hours. It is a tremendous waste of time which we can never regain. I am waiting patiently to see what the government will do.
I was exceedingly surprised and disappointed at the answer given to these men by the Minister of Labour. They wanted something concrete to take back to the men at Oshawa. They were asking for some suggestions from the government in regard to the solution of their difficulties, and the Minister of Labour said to them in effect: "I do not think you fellows should come to the government with your difficulties; you should iron them out yourselves." To me that was shocking. The only possible way these men have of ironing out any difficulties with the company is to go on strike. It is illegal to do that unless they comply with certain government regulations.
If they do comply with those regulations, then they are likely to be starved to death before the situation is solved. This is what happened in Kirkland Lake. Personally, I do not think that was the way in which this situation should have been handled. These men are desirous of cooperating with the government, and I do not believe we shall get anywhere in solving this production problem until there is complete coordination between the government and labour. There is to be set up before very long a war expenditures committee.

The Unemployment Insurance Act makes provision for the registration of persons out of work, and I believe that provision should be used for the purpose of keeping both members of parliament and the country advised from time to time, much in the same way as is done under the British act, regarding the number of unemployed in the country. We have never had any satisfactory statistics in Canada in connection with unemployment, but inasmuch as, under the Unemployment Insurance Act, all unemployed have to register at government offices, we should know from week to week or from month to month how many people are actually unemployed and what the unemployment situation is. If some member of the government would draw this matter to the attention of the Minister of Labour, I should be glad to let it go at that.

May I raise a question with regard to the Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminals. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) had, I know, intended to ask some questions and make a statement thereon, but in his unavoidable absence perhaps the minister would be good enough to make a statement to the committee.

The Prince Edward Island
car ferry is operated as a separate operation. Years ago it was included in the accounts of the Canadian National Railways, but some three or four years ago the car ferry was separated from the operation of the railway and a deficit item placed in the estimates. Evidently the amount placed in the estimates was a fairly close approximation to the deficit, and only a small additional amount is required.
The ferry is operated at a loss; and the greater the traffic, the greater the loss, in that additional trips cause increased expense.
As hon. members know, there were two ferries on the run, but unfortunately one was lost some months ago en route to Prince Edward Island from Saint John, where the boat had been overhauled. The boat sank in deep water. For a time it was thought it could be salvaged, but all the salvage operators have now examined the situation and decided that the boat could not be salvaged; consequently it was abandoned to the underwriters.
The position is that to keep up our war programme of shipbuilding and to rebuild the car ferry is impossible. The ways of one of our shipyards would have to be occupied for some fifteen months, and provision made to build special equipment. I suppose the building of that car ferry would interfere with the building of three or four standard 10,000 ton freighters. With the need for shipping so urgent, it is felt that the remaining ferry should perform the service until the war situation eases. In the meantime the one ferry is carrying on successfully. The operation has been normal this winter-I think there were one or two interruptions- but records show that there has never been a winter that there have not been interruptions for some twenty-four to thirty-six hours. I think the situation is one that can be allowed to continue until the war permits the replacement of that boat.

Does the minister anticipate that this one ferry will be able to take care of the spring and summer traffic, which, of course, will be much greater than in the winter? A considerable amount of agricultural produce comes across by that ferry, does it not?

The business has always been
taken care of by one ferry. It is only in very busy seasons, perhaps in August when the tourist traffic is heavy, that the two ferries are used. One is usually a standby for the other. The present ferry was the only means of communication with the island for a great many years, and it is felt that the one ferry should be able to handle the traffic this summer, because we expect there will be very little tourist traffic on account of the shortage of gasoline and rubber. A second ferry service to the island which operates during the summer months, has been greatly improved in the last two years. That service, from Woods island to Pictou, should relieve the strain considerably on the big ferry.

My colleague has not
referred to two matters which I regard as very important in connection with this ferry.
Interim Supply

He, of course, is the acting Minister of Transport. I have had some direct correspondence with both the minister and the Canadian National Railways. The president advised me some little time ago that after a good deal of examination they had found on the west coast a boat called the City of Sacramento which might possibly be available as a standby. I had been urging that if a new ferry could not be built, some boat be obtained in order to make absolutely sure that there would be no break-down in the service should anything happen to the present boat. The president of the railways realized the desirability of that situation being buttressed if at all possible, both because of the needs of the citizens of Prince Edward Island and the fact that there are two air training establishments on the island. The result is that at the present time there is going on an extensive examination with regard to obtain' ing the City of Sacramento, not only as to the terms on which she can be obtained, but also her fitness for use as a standby boat. She is not a car ferry, but she would provide desirable accommodation for a fill-in service.
While that examination has been going on, another project has come up, of transferring a car ferry from lake Michigan. The points about the use of that ferry were, first, whether or not she could get through the St. Lawrence canal locks, and it is found; that she cannot without having to be cut in two and put together again, as was done during the last war. The difficulty there is that in putting 'her together we would have to preempt for some little time a dock down the river, but it seems that situation is not insurmountable. The other point that has to be examined is whether the docks at cape Tormentine and Borden can be adapted1 to the boat or the boat to the docks. An examination is going on as to these two points. I have in my hand a letter from tlhe president of the company giving me the latest word, and the matter is being dealt with actively. I know that everything possible is being done to supplement the present service of the Price Edward Island with a standby or fill-in service by obtaining another boat.

In my judgment the past service was not very satisfactory. I have been to the island many times, and I cannot say I ever found the service wh'at I would call 100 per cent. In the first place it was difficult to get a car on the boat, and once you got it on, it was just as difficult to get it off. I am not sure whether it was the new boat or the old one that was lost-
The new boat.

Well, even as to the new one, I often intended to protest here about the difficulty one experienced in getting a motor car on and off the boat. The last time I went across that strait I scratched my car and jammed it a bit because of the narrow boat space. I hope, when the time comes that the government can build a new boat, they will build it large enough that people can come and go to the island without so mudh difficulty as in the past. If there were real accommodation for visitors to reach the island, instead of an arbitrary figure of 50,000 cars crossing in the season to that very beautiful island-nothing like it anywhere in America-it might be an arbitrary figure of 100,000, which would be a very good thing for business on the island. So I would say to the minister that when he comes to build a boat he should build it so that automobile traffic can be loaded and unloaded easily. I have seen lately in the Charlottetown Guardian reports of meetings of boards of trade and city councils-and I am not sure that the matter did not come up in the legislature-detailing the difficulties with which they are now faced. One boat will have very great difficulty in giving adequate service to those producing farm products on that island. Personally I have a very warm feeling for Prince Edward Island, because of its great beauty. There are no stones on the highways; there is beautiful rolling landscape everywhere. This country owes a lot to Prince Edward Island, and nothing should be left undone that might help give those people better transportation facilities than they have to-day.

A few weeks ago I wrote the Postmaster General about a matter of censorship concerning the city of Saint John. I have not a copy of that letter before me, but as I recollect them the facts were that a gentleman in Saint John had been corresponding with someone in the city of Boston. He came to the conclusion that there was a great deal of delay in the delivery of his letters, so to test the matter he wrote two letters at the same time, one of which was mailed in Saint John and the other taken to Montreal and mailed from there, both to the same address. The letter mailed from Montreal reached the addressee in Boston within a day or two; the letter mailed from Saint John did not reach Boston until about two weeks later.
I wonder whether the Postmaster General could give any explanation as to this very great delay.

I shall have an inquiry made, and shall be glad to give the hon. member an answer to-morrow. I have no information at the moment, but I shall endeavour to get it as quickly as possible.

Interim Supply

Could the Postmaster
General give us any information as to the postal situation in Westboro? That suburban area has been extensively built up within the last three years, and a year ago last Christmas an unsatisfactory state of affairs existed in regard to postal delivery. During the past year some steps were taken to improve the situation, but they were grossly inadequate and quite unsatisfactory. That area is virtually an extension of the city of Ottawa. There is a mail service along the main streets, but no service further on. Many of the residents of that community have to walk a mile or two miles for their mail, and have to wait an hour or two before getting it. Sometimes they have to wait as long as three days for their mail. I believe it is the policy of the government not to extend the mail service any more than is absolutely necessary in these days, but actually this would be simply an extension of an already existing service. The municipal authorities of that area have gone to the extent of makin-g provision for clearing the streets, numbering the houses, renaming the streets and everything else in order to get this service, and the situation is getting more serious all the time.
Let me give an example. Recently a constituent of mine who was working in Shawini-gan Falls received a letter from the Department of National Defence asking him to report for military training. The letter had been expected, and calls had been made at the post office every day for it. It took seven days to arrive from Toronto and be delivered to the recipient, which left him only nine days in which to make his arrangements to answer the summons. I quote this as one isolated instance, but it is only one of many. I say that an area like Westboro, the home of so many business people and civil servants who require efficient mail service, should not have-to put up with this deplorable situation. So I would ask the Postmaster General to reconsider the matter, which I have already discussed with him, and to which he gave a favourable heaiing. I feel it my bounden duty to continue urging him until his pleasant reception, and the pleasant smile he is now giving me, are crystallized into the desired action in that community.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I want to take this opportunity of saying a few words on this resolution. I realize that opportunities will be given after the Easter recess to discuss the appropriation, of which this forms a part, and I should hope that at that time we may have the debate so well organized that it will not necessitate all the ministers remaining here during the whole discussion, and that we may be able to deal with our problems department by department and perhaps facilitate business in that way. I wish to say a few words on the matter which was brought before us yesterday and which forms part of the programme for the year for which this appropriation is being made. In further explanation, I would say that I do not expect to be here to-morrow, and I crave the indulgence of the house to permit me to say what I have to say at this time.
The war has necessitated many drastic measures being introduced into the house, but 1 suppose that nothing more drastic has been suggested to the country than the recent outline for the mobilization of man-power. We realize that this war must be a total war if we are going to win it, and again I should like to say as emphatically as I can that a total war involves much more than the mobilization of human labour power. Without the mobilization of our resources upon the same basis and at the same time we shall not get an enthusiastic all-out war effort in Canada. Moreover, we are fighting for the democratic way of life, and the proposals made in this house the day before yesterday were of such a nature that they involve the setting aside, at least for a considerable time, of many of the ordinary procedures of democracy.
I hope the determination that we have seen here from time to time to defend individual enterprise in the midst of this war will not be continued to the detriment of our war effort. Hon. members probably saw' in the Ottawa Journal this evening a description of the manner in which a great
monopoly in the United States, the Standard Oil company of New Jersey, represented in this country by Imperial Oil Limited, handled a secret process for the making of synthetic rubber. That process was handed over to Germany and everything was done up to yesterday to prevent the use of the patents, even in connection with the war effort of the United States. I want to say that that kind of attitude brings home to us as forcibly as it could be brought home the danger of allowing great monopolies to control, in peace and in war, the vital resources of the countries in which we live. I have noticed that some of the people connected with these organizations, and some hon. gentlemen in this house, have stated again and again that we must preserve individual enterprise in our war effort. It has been amazing to me to hear some people from their places here demand that we shall not interfere more than necessary with private business, that we shall continue the individual enterprise system, and then demand mobilization on a compulsory basis of the labour power of our men and women. In this great crisis we are not objecting to the compulsory mobilization of labour power, but we say that if we are to have equality of sacrifice, there must be a mobilization of our industrial and economic resources upon the same basis and at the same time.
I wish to object to the manner in which the sweeping proposals were introduced into this house. Orders in council of the most sweeping nature, already finally approved by the government, have been placed before this house while it has been sitting. During the war we have found that immediately before the house assembled on one or two occasions, and while the house was sitting on other occasions, policies of the most mndamental nature have been placed before the house in the form of orders in council, without any opportunity being given to parliament to discuss the various phases of the proposals being made.
I am not arguing that in the midst of war it is always advisable to introduce, in a manner permitting of long discussion, new policies which may interfere with business or with people. But I do say that when it is necessary to introduce policies suddenly by order in council a certain period should be set aside immediately so that this house may discuss their implications. It may not be proper and it may not be easy to make any changes in those policies, but in almost every instance the government is empowered to make regulations to carry out
War Appropriation

the policy and at least we should have an opportunity of discussing the policies before the regulations are made.
As I said, this is a matter which affects the lives of all Canadian people more than anything else we have done. In my opinion, it is too important a matter to be the subject of a mere governmental decree. We should have had a bill which we could have discussed section by section. I think this matter might have been introduced in such a way as to make unnecessary a very long discussion. To some extent I understand why certain measures of this description are introduced in the way they are. We have had some rather long discussions on some things that perhaps did not require such lengthy debate.
I am going to throw out a suggestion which hon. members may think over. We have admired the manner in which during this great war crisis the British parliament has justified itself as an institution. Its rules differ materially from our own. Perhaps the time has come when this house should set up a committee to study the rules followed in the British House of Commons and see if we could not adapt some of those rules to our own needs. In that way we might have a different type of discussion, just as free but not as prolonged as the discussions that have occurred during this war period. I said a few moments ago that there are many ways in which prolonged discussion might be obviated, but I think a measure of this description should be given all the consideration we can give it, and at once.
I notice from the public press that the head of one of the great labour organizations in this country has stated that labour will give every cooperation to the government in carrying out this policy, but he regretted that the labour movement had not been consulted on this policy before it was introduced into this house. In my opinion, the representatives of the people's organizations should have been taken into the confidence of the government and the whole question thoroughly discussed with the labour organizations, the farmer organizations, the legion and other organizations vitally interested in the mobilization of labour. In any event, whether or not these organizations were called into consultation, surely there was no reason why parliament should be ignored in the manner in which parliament was and has been ignored on so many occasions during this war. I have followed the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) over a number of years both before and since coming into this house, and if there is one man in the public life of

this country who has talked about the supremacy of parliament and the need1 for parliament to decide, it is the Prime Minister himself. Yet again and again policies of vital importance are adopted by order in council without parliament being consulted at all, and we have the latest example in the measure to which I have just referred.
I want to protest, too, against the manner in which this measure has been introduced into the house at this late hour just before the Easter recess. The government orders on to-day's order paper, although we have managed to dispose of some of them this afternoon and this evening, are still pretty well filled with important measures or have been right up to to-night. Consequently members have refrained from entering on a discussion of this measure. Yet this policy has long been under consideration by the government. I remember reading a speech made by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) in Montreal as long ago as last December in which a measure such as this was clearly foreshadowed. I looked over a summary of the minister's speech yesterday and found that the orders in council which have been passed bringing into effect this new policy were also clearly foreshadowed: and almost accurately outlined by the minister when 'he spoke in Montreal as far back as last December. Therefore this policy has been under consideration by the government for some time, and there was no reason, to my mind, why the organizations I have mentioned should not have been called into consultation before the policy was decided upon, and certainly no reason why some discussion of it should not have taken place in this 'house.
Why the haste now, when we have not yet provided employment for some of our workers who are at present unemployed? The hon-. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) this afternoon read into the record an advertisement which appeared in the local press from an automobile workers' organization pointing out that there were many technical men in that organization who are unemployed to-day. There are some hundreds more unemployed at Kirkland Lake, many others at Kitchener, and there are men working short time, I am told, in a number of industries throughout the country. While it may be essential to organize our men and our women, we should first have utilized fully the labour power and the machinery that we have already available before a measure of this sort is adopted by order in council.
I know that the total war effort which must be waged in order to bring us to victory involves some sort of intelligent selective

War Appropriation
service, but an intelligent selective service not only for men and. women but for industries as well, and I want not only on my own behalf but on behalf of those associated with me, to protest in the strongest possible manner against the way in which these important proposals have been introduced at this time.
I do not wish to go into the problem at great length. There are some features of the legislation that are interesting, and not only interesting but worthy of commendation. I would commend the attempt to provide labour for the farm. But in saying that, I am not sure about the justice or rightness of taking one particular class out from under the selective service system. I am not sure that it is either wise or proper; it may cause grave antagonisms between groups. Agricultural labour has to be provided, and the condition of the farmer to-day is such that he cannot compete with industry for labour. His prices are too low and wages too high in relation to his prices, although not too high in relation to the cost of living and the cost of other things. But the young farmer, the farmer's son, by this legislation is kept on the farm, and no matter how low his standard of living may be, he is prohibited from seeking work in any other industry unless he obtains permission. So not only have you frozen farm labour on the farm at a comparatively low wage level, with farmer's prices at least in the prairie provinces too low to enable them even to operate, let alone pay a decent and reasonable wage, but you have said to the young men engaged in that industry: You must remain where you are unless you agree to enlist voluntarily in the armed forces. One of the criticisms I would make of the proposals is that in my opinion they doom the farmer to the sort of peasantry in which he has lived for a considerable time, and doom the farm labourer to a sort of peonage as compared with other forms of labour in this country.
In the working out of these selective service measures, who will control the operation of the policy? That, I think, is a vital question. I notice that a director and an assistant director have been appointed. I do not know either of these gentlemen, but I presume they are worth-while citizens of this country and probably very able men in their own spheres. But one is an engineer and company director, and the other is a stockbroker. The two people who will head this selective service system are, first, a company engineer, and second, a stockbroker. Where are the representatives of the people who are going to be regimented? Where are the representatives
of labour? Where are the representatives of the farmer? Where are the representatives of the common people?
I say to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) to-night that while I think he has done a remarkable job in many respects in organizing, nevertheless I have been alarmed at the trend in his department to the control of all our activities by powerful business men or by dollar-a-year men who are close to big business and big-business organizations. Our people are becoming suspicious of this sort of thing.
This is another mistake which the government has made in selecting men-no matter how good personally they may be-who have the wrong sort of association to command the right sort of confidence and support all across the country. The same is true of the manner in which it is proposed to grant the appeals. We have to-day national service appeal boards throughout the country. I am not going into the boards separately to-night, but in my opinion, from personal observation, some of the boards that have been set up have not commanded the confidence of democratically-minded people, and such boards are not the type that should be entrusted with this new power. If they were set up originally to select men who may be suitable for military training and to decide those who should get training or those who should be exempted, that does not qualify them for deciding whether a man is suitable for a certain type of industry or not. We require a new form of board, and the government should look over the personnel of the boards set up and endeavour to give a much wider sort of representation on those boards than we have had up to the present time.
We have, of course, the national advisory board, and the Prime Minister told us that provision would be made for the representation of women's organizations and other bodies upon such a board. That is all to the good, but so far the national labour relations board has not been functioning as it should have done. Then again, the selection of those who will be chosen for various types of work is left to officers to be located in the various cities, and unless these officers are selected with the greatest care we shall find that there will be a great deal of discontent with regard to them. I suggest to the government that before this mobilization goes into effect, on every board there should be adequate representation of the people's organizations, such as the labour and farmer organizations, the legion, if you will, and other organizations which represent great masses of the people of Canada.
War Appropriation

Another thing that struck me about this measure is the fact that if a young man has been turned down on account of physical unfitness, he may get medical aid and hospitalization so that he may be taken into the army. If it is necessary to give hospitalization and medical aid to bring up to efficiency a man going into the army, ought it not to be equally wise to give the same medical treatment and hospitalization to men and women so that they may be rendered efficient in industry as well? I should like to see the government provide medical aid and treatment for those who fall below the proper physical level both in industry and in the armed forces-men and women. Let me say in connection with this problem that the orders in council do provide for the payment of transportation to women if they are going to take work in industry. I suggest that we should have a comprehensive plan so that when men and women are moved from one place to another, where their labour is required for war purposes, we should look after the transportation problem so far as they are concerned and make some family allowance if they are compelled to be away from home. That, may I add, is being done in Great Britain where they move people around from place to place for the purpose of industry.

This is, indeed, a drastic mobilization of human power. On more than one occasion the Prime Minister has told us that the government intended to use ' the power now in its hands, under the National Resources Mobilization Act, to mobilize industry and wealth; but in spite of all that may be said, the fact is that industry and wealth are not yet mobilized to the extent to which it is proposed now to mobilize human power. In whose interests is this labour power being organized? In the interests of the country? Yes; but at the same time, under the present economic set-up, we are mobilizing labour for the National Steel Car Company, for General Motors, for Chrysler and for Ford. I say that we ought to mobilize these corporations on the same basis and on the same terms; then we should have something approaching equality of sacrifice. We have not that equality to-day, no matter what ministers may say.

I suppose all members of this house must have observed, from the balance sheets these days, how prosperous some of these companies are. They must have noticed the very expensive advertising these companies are undertaking. All members, I know, a few days ago received a very expensively framed copy of an advertisement that had been published during the recent victory loan campaign. I have not written to thank General Motors for the nice picture to hang in my office; I feel I ought to write and thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), because that advertising will be charged up to profits-excess profits-and eight-five per cent of the cost of that framed picture and that type of advertising will, in fact, be paid by the people of Canada, because the government of Canada will not collect the excess profits tax on money which is spent in that manner.

We have not yet begun to mobilize wealth and industry. If we are to have equality of sacrifice, that must be brought about without delay. If we are to have an enthusiastic war effort it must be achieved without further delay.
I do not intend to delay the discussion any longer, but I want to emphasize with all the force I can, first, that the method of introducing policies of this kind is undemocratic. It is unfortunate. It does not give members of this house an opportunity to do what they are sent here to do. Secondly, if we are going to mobilize the human power of this nation, it must be mobilized under the supervision of the people themselves, supervised by representatives that they themselves choose. To-day in Canada we have organizations which choose representatives of the people for the people, other than this House of Commons. I refer, of course, to the great nation-wide labour and farmer organizations. When we have done that, as my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said this afternoon, we should guarantee to the men who are mobilized and engaged in these industries the right to bargain collectively through organizations of their own choice.
When we were in Great Britain I asked Mr. Bevin, the British Minister of Labour, as to the status of collective bargaining in Great Britain. He replied, "Oh, well, to-day that has become a part of our constitution." When I asked him the further question as to whether in government-owned plants or government partly owned and controlled plants normal labour organization was permitted he said, "Well, our great naval dockyards are, of course, government-owned; our civilian workers are organized in the union of their choice." Then with a smile he added, "And I am a national secretary of that union."
If we are to have a satisfactory and enthusiastic war effort, we have to safeguard the rights of the common people to .determine through their organizations their own activities and their own way of life to a larger extent than we have in past days. Indeed, we have to go further than that; there must be some joint management of industry between the present management and labour. Only in that way can we get an all-out, complete and enthusiastic war effort.
So, then, in making this appropriation, one-quarter of the $2,000,000,000 estimate for this coming year, I want to impress upon the
government that we shall not get the all-out effort required to win this war unless we and the other democratic nations can organize ourselves completely and efficiently. The totalitarian powers have done that; they have done it in a manner which we detest. I am one who believes that under our democratic institutions we can organize our countries as efficiently as, and much more enthusiastically than the totalitarian powers can ever do if we only take the people into our confidence and show them that we are prepared to give them a square deal. Equality of sacrifice demands that the people's organizations shall have a voice in all the war activities of this nation, and that the great industrial concerns of this country shall be mobilized, selected, conscripted if you will, in the same manner and upon the same terms and at the same time as we mobilize human labour.

speechtext:
I
would not be true to the character of my representation in this house or to my convictions in this matter if I did not rise at once to support in the main the observations of the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Coldwell). I believe that among hon. members on all sides, of the house there is a growing conviction that if we are to make our prosecution of this war what we all want it to be in a world in flames, there must not be on the part of any group in this country any suspicion of the loyalty and good faith of other groups in the country. I represent a constituency largely engaged in the automobile industry, which is at the present time, as to the Ford plant namely, and to only a relatively less extent at the Chrysler plant in Windsor, engaged in a total way in the production of military vehicles of all kinds that are being used to wage this war. I think that, generally speaking, labour has a legitimate complaint about its representation on important boards that are being set up. There has not been thus far, because this measure was introduced before any opportunity for discussion in parliament was presented, any real opportunity for members of this house to discuss the proposals for the mobilization of man-power announced the other day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Labour has complained, and the responsible type of labour leadership has complained, that it was not represented on important boards. It is not too late now for the administration to include on boards of selection, boards that will deal with postponements and exemptions, not only the representatives of industry-they should be there-but, as well, representatives of labour and of the farming community as well as of the legion
16S0
War Appropriation

and other such organizations. The time has come when there should be on the part of labour and of industry less suspicion of one another than there has been in the past. I have heard it said by various people in this house; I have heard it in the corridors; I have heard some of my own people whom I represent say, "Oh, we cannot trust these men." If in this country we have reached the point where labour is not to be trusted, that is a terrible indictment of the nationhood of this country. I do not believe that. As I said a moment ago, I represent a constituency *which contains a huge proportion of labouring men. I know them. I come from that group myself and, indeed, I believe practically every member of this house in some way or another owes his inheritance to people of that kind. At the present time my own father is engaged in a factory making munitions of war. Am I to say that I do not trust him? And he is no different from the thousands of men who are engaged in the war factories of this country.
So I say, with all the sincerity and all the force of which I am capable, that the time has come when we should recognize that if there is a partnership in industry-and we have talked about that for years-we should make it a real partnership. Let us give labour full representation on these boards. Let us also give the farming community full representation. I am sure we shall not find that, as a result, any of the so-called radical groups will take advantage of the situation. We can trust the labouring people of this country; and by trusting them we shall help develop the sort of labour leadership, the kind of responsibility in leadership, which so many people in Canada find lacking in connection with labour in this country at the present time.
I fully agree with what the hon. member has just said with regard to the right of collective bargaining. The government of this country recognizes that right, so we are not asking for something that is new. Collective bargaining is a technique that is older than any member of this house, and it has kept the industrial peace of more countries than one could count on one's ten fingers. The preservation of the industrial peace of England has been maintained largely because the British government and industry and labour in Britain have fostered the development of a tradition under which not only employees but employers themselves would not for a moment think of resorting to any other technique. Recently, in my own city of Windsor we had a committee to carry on the victory loan campaign. On that committee were found not only representatives of industry but also representatives of labour

and of the farming community; and in that campaign the labouring people, fourteen thousand of them in one plant alone, invested their money just as willingly as did the management of those plants. So, if they can be trusted in a victory loan campaign, surely we can trust them in these other endeavours.
I say these things because I think we on this side of the house who represent the traditions of Liberalism should not hesitate, when the opportunity is presented as it is to-night, to properly enunciate our principles. I agree in the main with what has been just said; and I am satisfied that if this house gave a similar concurrence, if there were an attitude of trust on the part of labour toward industry and on the part of industry toward labour, we would not have the suspicion and the lack of unity which still exist in the industrial world.

I am not going to speak of that matter now, but I hope the work of that committee will bring about many of the results to which reference has been made already this evening. Certainly, after the war no such unemployment as has existed heretofore should be permitted. That matter may not come under this resolution, but much has been said about the organization of industry, and I am one of those who believe that industry should be organized so that, after the war, unemployment will be a thing of the past.
Since I have been very closely associated with working men for more than a quarter of a century, naturally their hopes and desires have always been foremost in my mind. Many industries, I know, have within their own organizations what they call sick benefit or medical assistance plans, whereby any of their employees who become sick or incapacitated receive assistance. That is not government assistance, however, and I am convinced that the time has come for the government to consider adopting the methods prevailing in the old country, under which.

War Appropriation
all working men in all plants, not only in those having their own organizations, shall receive sick benefits and medical assistance. I would say that was the second thing that should be provided after the war.
Furthermore, as I look back over the last ten years and recall the number of cases that have come to my attention of workmen losing their homes through no fault of their own, I hope that sort of thing will not prevail after the wrar either. Men who for years saved out of their humble wages and salaries acquired homes, perhaps not fully paid for, and then during the depression, which was not the result of any fault of theirs, they lost those homes. That is a situation which must not be allowed to prevail after the war.
I agree with what was said by the two previous speakers, that the time has come when we all-for I believe every member of this house is just as much interested as I am

must see to it that the conditions which obtained in the past shall not prevail again, and that our working men may receive that to which they are entitled. I hope, as has beqn suggested, that some modus operandi will be worked out under which these most desirable aims may be realized.

May I add just a word, to deal with what has been said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). There seems to be some misapprehension with regard to the mobilization plan, particularly with reference to its application to labour and the part labour will play in connection with the administration of it. May I point out to my hon. friends, to the house and to the country that this system of national selective service is being operated by the Department of Labour, which is presided over by a man who is as well known in labour circles as any man in Canada, and who, indeed, has made his reputation in connection with labour. I do not feel at this stage that anyone should have any apprehension that labour will not be wholly, fairly and properly represented in connection with the administration of this measure.
May I say this, that having in mind my position and responsibility, someone might have suggested that it might have been administered by the Department of National Defence, simply because of the fact that in respect of the men needed for the army we have a heavy interest in it. That was not done. It might have been administered by the Department of National War Services, but that was not done. It was placed with the
Department of Labour, and I believe that all labour men in this country will realize that that was a recognition of the fact that they are very much a partner in this war, and that their rights and their responsibilities would be respected by this government.
May I add, as my colleague the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) has pointed out to me, that many of the functions of the Department of National War Services were transferred to the Department of Labour in order that this national selective service system might be worked out with the full appreciation and full cooperation of labour.
Then, mention has been made of boards. I do not know what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had in mind. The only boards we know of are, in the first place, the employment offices which will be operated throughout the country-and operated by the Department of Labour, under the Minister of Labour. They will be operated by men who understand the problems of labour and who have been acting in connection with it. Then, if there are advisory committees throughout the country, those advisory committees most assuredly will have on them representatives of labour. I am sure the house and the country, and particularly our friends who represent labour, can be assured that they will have the fullest representation in connection with anything which has to do with the administration of this legislation. With that assurance I feel the house will be satisfied. I should not want the wrong impression to go out from the debate which has taken place to-night, or from the speeches which have been made, that labour has been overlooked. It seems to me that labour at least is recognized fully in connection with the administration, and will be recognized in connection with the organization and set-up which will be put into effect throughout this country.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) very well stated the case for the group he leads in the house. May I point out that having been a worker myself, and having been associated with the trades union movement for a considerable number of years, I know the attitude of the average working man to-day to the national selective service programme as proposed by

the government. There is a suspicion on their part, and that suspicion is well founded. It is based on the attitude of those who, we know, at the present time are in charge of organizing the national selective service of the working people of this country.
The 'hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has stated that to date we know an engineer has been appointed, as representative of the companies. Another gentleman is one whose qualifications no one doubts, but whose environment and background are not reassuring. They are to take care of the problems of the people who are to be regimented. Many, many times I have heard it said1 in the house that the government recognizes the rights of labour and favours collective bargaining. We can judge that statement only on the basis of the government's approach to that problem in the past. I want to say this, that it is anything but reassuring.
Only 15 per cent of the workers in this country are organized. Eighty-five per cent of them are unorganized, because of their opposition to organization. Very recently we have had a demonstration of just about what the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) will do with respect to the enforcement of the rights of workers who organize. Kirkland Lake is a blot on his administration. It will take a long time to remove from that department the stigma of what happened there. I shall not go into it in detail, because the story is well known. They obeyed the wishes of the government and the laws of the land. They endeavoured to lay down their organization, with the result that, according to the last information I had, a thousand of them were without jobs and without relief. Nothing -has been done about it, so far as I know.
Another thing I should like to call to the attention of the house is -this: Many, many times, from many platforms and over the radio I have heard the statement made that one of the first things -which would1 come in Canada or any democratic country, in the event of totalitarian nations winning the war, would be the loss of trades unions. I want someone to explain to me what is the difference in the mentality of a person who destroys a trades union, and one who will not allow it to be born. In 'my opinion, there is no difference at all.
Furthermore, an active campaign has been carried on by industrialists in Canada, since the outbreak of the war, to offset the formation of any kind of legitimate trades unions functioning in this country. I am ashamed of such tactics. In the press from time to time and in the house hon. members have risen in their places to point out the relationship
[Mr. Gillis.3
between this country and our good neighbour to the south. It has been said that if we are going to get through this struggle successfully, Canada and that good neighbour must have a common understanding, and no differences of opinion. We are in this fight, all the way-both Canada and the United States. But at the same time big business directorates interlock between this country and the United States. Nothing is done about that. It is said that it is legitimate business, and it passes. Manufacturers' associations can organize on both sides of the boundary line, and lay down international organization rules. But just as soon as a representative of labour comes from the United States to Canada and endeavours to employ the experience he has gained over many years in a similar field in the United States, when he sets foot on Canadian soil he is accused at once of being a foreigner. It is said that he is a foreign agitator, and the press of Canada from one end of the country to the other goes to great lengths to build up the idea that a "foreign agitator is in Sudbury creating a disturbance."
Only just recently the Canadian offices of the mine, mill and smelter workers' union, with headquarters in the United States, were destroyed. This was a respectable group associated with that organization, a group which was endeavouring only to give the Canadian worker the benefit of their experience. The men were prepared to organize to carry out an all-out war effort. But one of these men, who is accused of being a foreign agitator, was beaten up and placed in a hospital. There were screaming headlines in a large section of the press.
I call this to the attention of the Minister of National Defence, because he has a serious job to do, and we want to help him.

This thing is becoming a joke. If this thing is only a gesture, there is no use in wasting any time on it; but if this national selective service is to be a success, it will be necessary to get all possible help in order to put it over. The miners' unions in the east will be ready to work with you. I say that any industry operator who retards collective bargaining, who refuses to take in the men round the table with him, is throwing away one of the greatest assets he has. If General Motors is going to operate this thing; if you deny the workers the right to sit in at these councils and help out with this war effort, it will not be a success.
Yesterday I met twenty men from the automotive industry. These men were workers; they were not officials or salaried men. But they were alarmed at the lack of production in their industry. They had sent a committee here to Ottawa to find out what could be done to step up production and to make the industry work. They were here to offer their services. If you do not want them to work with you, that is all right, but I say that the first requirement is to have these men sit in with the boss. If a boss is afraid to meet his employees, then there is something wrong with his business. If the worker is going to be a

partner, then he should1 sit round the conference table to study these problems. If we are going to beat Mr. Hitler and the Japs, there must be some understanding on that basis. Our people have gone through a lot of misery. Only 15 per cent of the workers of this country have been permitted to organize. That is not good enough. Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate, but I am prompted to do so by what has been said in some of the speeches here to-night. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) claims that he has been living in a different atmosphere from that in which those who administer some of the laws of Canada live. When I hear labour exponents argue their case I often wonder who is really the labouring man. Labour includes a large proportion of the population of this dominion, and there are certain elements in this country who seem to think that they have a divine right, that they can enjoy all the rights of society without undertaking any of its obligations.
If we are going to have an all-out war effort, it is necessary and essential that we should all contribute according to our ability,

that we should give the very best that is in us and not always be looking to find fault with what the other fellow is doing. We should see that we do our own job and do it right.
I have not armed myself to-night with figures beyond those I have charged my memory with, taken from news items, but I should like to take a few moments to reply to some of the things which have been said. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) waxed eloquent over the contribution of labour and criticized the shortcomings of the financiers. Mr. Speaker, I am not a financier. I live among about the same class of people as those represented by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the common people who are in the great majority, and, after all, an expression from a representative of the common people should have its weight. I am going to give my view as I see it from the point of view of the ordinary, honest-to-goodness farmer who labours, I think, just as much as any organized labour man that I know of. I think, too, that we should appreciate those in this country who work in an executive capacity. It is foolish to suppose that because these men wear white collars they are not working men. I know a lot of people in the city in my constituency who are sitting up nights over the financial problem of seeing that those men who work from eight to five shall have some place to sell their labour.	These people deserve some
recognition, especially in our war effort, and I am prepared, too, to pay a high tribute to industry for the wonderful contribution it has made to our war effort.
The Monetary Times in the month of January published a record of the business done in 1942 by firms with seats on the Montreal and Toronto stock exchanges and showed that although these firms had to do a great deal more business than they did during the preceding year, their dividends amounted to only five million dollars more than the year before. In spite of doing almost double the volume of business, a large part of their profits were taken away from them by the excess profits tax legislation and corporation taxes brought down in the early part of this war. Therefore these firms are more or less tax-collecting agencies for the government. It is wise to let them have a reasonable profit because 85 per cent of the profit made by corporations is collected for the war effort of this country. I know it is not popular to defend finance, but it is more easy for me to do so because I am not a financier myself. I try to look upon the question from the common-sense point of view that there should be harmony

War Appropriation
and a proper relationship between the industrial man, the labour man, the farmer, and the executive who are all working together in this all-out war effort that we have to make. I think it is hardly becoming to champion one particular class of our people as if they possessed all the virtues, although I have a great deal of sympathy with labour.

speechtext:
That is true, and we should try to keep a proper perspective.
My Social Credit friends in the far corner of the house are exponents of a new order in finance. They make a special attack on our existing financial institutions. I am a practical man, Mr. Speaker, and have to look at things from results as I see them in a practical way, and so I shall not attempt to go into their monetary theory. But let me point out this to my Social Credit friends. I see by the Financial Post to-day that the net profit of the chartered banks last year was about $13,500,000. The net profit of the banks would be what it would probably cost the nation for the banks to be the bookkeepers of the nation, and in spite of what hon. gentlemen said about our financial institutions being parasites, and so forth, $13,500,000 represents only one-quarter of one per cent of our total national wealth if we accept the figure of $6,000,000,000 as the estimated national wealth of the whole country. Suppose the social credit theory were put into practice and we had what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar advocates-tax-free money. You would have to pay for the cost of doing that business. At the present time the interest charged remunerates the banks and allows them to pay their staffs. The interest charge is their profit motive. So the net profit of the banks represents only what it costs the public for the banks to be the bookkeepers of the nation. I thought it was time that somebody should rise in his place in this house and turn over the leaf so that we could see the other side of the picture. I am not here to defend the banks or any financial institutions whatsoever. I am just trying to use the ordinary common sense the Lord has seen fit to give me and to vision this thing from the point of view of a practical man.
Our Social Credit friends in the far corner of this house also dwell on the new order there is going to be after the war. But I say to them, do not be carried away by any false hopes, for I do not think this new order will ever take away the struggle from life, and I think it is well to keep that in mind. It is all very well to find fault with some of the things we have with us to-day under our present system, but very often, you know, it is
difficult to put something better in their place. I would also give this word of warning to the same hon. gentlemen, that when you have this new order, you will still find the same elements among us complaining about it, because no matter what kind of new order is brought into being, there will always be those who will make the best of it and finally find their way to the top, and then we shall have the same element we have to-day wanting another new order. But why do we need to argue about the new order while the war is on? Why not postpone that discussion and see if we cannot make a job of winning the war against the most vile and vicious enemy that ever befouled this earth? That is what I have been thinking, and I have been waiting for some man more able than I to discuss these matters. Perhaps they were too modest, and with me it may be a case of "fools rush in where angels fear to tread." Nevertheless that happens to be my nature. I generally champion the cause of the underdog, and I believe that when you have a friend who needs protection it is better to do it behind his back than before his face.
While the banks and industry have not been making excessive profits, labour, I believe, is getting as fair a share of the wealth of this country to-day as any class. If there is any preference, it is the labouring class that gets the preference, as compared with the farmer and industry. This war has been carried on upon the basis of a 3 per cent war. The last war was a 5J per cent war; therefore even finance is taking its cut this time. That is something which ought to be considered. Furthermore, while we have been at war for two and a half years, there is no evidence, so far as I can see, that one man in the dominion has become a millionaire or one firm has made millions in consequence of the war. We have taken the glamour of profiteering out of the war, and I am also prepared to say that a great deal of the opposition to the government-why do we not do this, and why do we not do that?-is due to the fact that a certain element of society in the sountry are disappointed that they cannot get their hands in up to the elbow and make themselves millionaires. A great deal of the criticism of the efforts of the administration could, I believe, be traced to that very reason. I regret that I did not come here a little better prepared to contribute to the debate, but I could not sit here any longer and allow some of the things that we have heard to go unchallenged.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to the Kirkland Lake strike. Perhaps he is more familiar with organized labour
War Appropriation

than I am, but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that his view of the strike is not shared generally in the part of Ontario from which I come. I may be wrong, but I think that when the men who have enjoyed the distinction of having from 20 to 25 per cent more for their labour than the labour men in the rest of the country, assert themselves at this time in the manner in which they have done, they do not do organized labour any good, nor do they enhance themselves in the estimation of the Canadian people. The hon. member can argue all he likes, but I suggest to him that the less said on this subject, the better. Let it die down, and the next time these men attempt to organize, let them see to it that they do not repeat the mistakes which they have made in the past. Let it go by the board; that would be my advice.

I venture to say that such hon. members would come back into the house better informed. I am prompted to say what I am saying now because I have gathered a considerable amount of the information which I am giving to-night as a result of my associations with these people. As I say, I can talk their language and they can talk mine as well.
I regret having taken up so much time, but I could not sit here quietly without coming to the defence of people who apparently have no one to speak for them. Not that I am interested in the industrialists of the country, but I would remind the house that we need all phases of the economic order if we are to make this a happy and comfortable place to live in. After all, happiness is what we are all after. I would suggest another bit of philosophy to my friends. They may argue as long as they like about finances, they may talk as much as they like about the dollar; but happiness is a homemade product and it cannot be made out of dollars and cents.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
May I answer the charge which the hon. gentleman has made, that criticisms of the government's efforts can be traced to those who have not been able to get their hands up to the elbow into the pool of profits. Apparently he understands the language and mentality of those who think their main object in life is to get their noses into the trough at the expense of their fellowmen who are contributing to the welfare of the nation by their sweat and toil. I want him to know now that we in this part of the house at least, in our efforts to represent labour, will have nothing to do with that sort of thing.
I make this criticism of the government's action. I say to them: You have mobilized labour, but you have left industry and finance unmobilized. The people of Canada wanted complete mobilization of the country in total war; you have brought down orders in council, and the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) confirms it-mobilizing man-power, the labour of the country. But there has been nothing so far as we can see to show that you intend to have the factories continue operating. This war will likely be won or lost on the production lines of industry.

War Appropriation
It is equipment that we need. Labour in Canada is showing itself willing to lbe mobilized if you will produce the machines, but nothing is done to see that the factories are kept operating. General Motors can close down, or the aeroplane plants can close down production or slow down, and the shipbuilding yards can slow down, but there is nothing in the way of mobilizing industry so tlhat parliament and the government of the country can demand that plants keep working day and night.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Will my hon. friend explain how we could mobilize industry?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: See that the plants of the country are working day and night.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Are they not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Many of them are not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Where?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
One in Ottawa. Oshawa was closing down, and a thousand men in Kirkland Lake are doing nothing. I do not know why they should be digging for gold anyway; they would be better employed producing tanks and aeroplanes.
This government claims that it has representatives of labour operating the mobilization work. I say that men who left labour and organized labour and have been in the pay of the government for years do not properly represent labour. What needs to be done first of all, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has said, is to get labour organized and then let labour and farm organizations select their own men to represent them on the board, not for a government which has prevented labour from organizing for forty years to go out and select those whom it probably knows from their position will carry out the will of their masters. A partnership between labour and industry as it is operated to-day is like a partnership between the cat and the canary; the canary ends inside the cat. What we need to solve this problem of labour is to have on these advisory boards men selected by labour to act as labour's representatives in directing policy. Labour must be a part owner of industry, just as the people of Canada feel that the natural resources of this country are the birthright of the Canadian people.
Labour will be more efficient when it is organized. There are fewer strikes when labour is organized. Organized labour is satisfied labour, because they know that if they have not their rights they have at least the machinery with which they can work in a democratic way for those rights. What has happened in Kirkland Lake in the past few
months is a disgrace to a country or a government which claims that in any way it has the interests of labour at heart.

Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second times, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I anticipate that there will
be some debate on this. To keep the record straight, I should say that at some early stage I shall have to move or have one of my colleagues move to reduce this amount from $2,000,000,000 to $1,500,000,000 because of the fact that a bill has just been passed voting one-quarter of the amount by way of interim supply. But I do not think I need do that to-night; it may be that I should not do that until the $500,000,000 bill has passed parliament as a whole. It is on this particular measure and at this stage that the defence ministers make their statements and we try to lay the basis for an orderly discussion of the war effort of the government. speechtext: May I ask if in this statement the minister is going to make any reference to the two new divisions to which the Prime Minister referred?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the minister mind explaining the difference between recurring and non-recurring items?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Generally speaking, nonrecurring are capital expenditures; recurring, to use a colloquialism, might be called operating expenses. That does not perhaps apply 
to departmental expenditures generally, but it indicates the rough division between the two terms.
On January 26, I think it was, the Prime Minister indicated what our programme was for 1942-43. I dealt with the same matter also at some length, so I shall not take time

War Appropriation
to go over that again except to remind the committee, so that we may get a running start, that we have the first, second and third infantry divisions overseas, together with the fifth armoured division, and an army tank brigade. We have the fourth division in Canada. These are all active units. The proposal is, and the programme for this year is, to convert the fourth infantry division into an armoured division and to mobilize an army tank brigade, which will be in addition to the army tank brigade which is now overseas. The expectation is to dispatch the fourth armoured division and the army tank brigade which is to be mobilized, together with a considerable number of corps and army troops, overseas during this year, so that if the programme is carried out, our overseas representation will be five divisions, two of which will be armoured divisions and three of which will be infantry divisions, together with two army tank brigades.
Those are the formations. In addition, there will be a very substantial number of army troops, and corps troops, that is to say, on lines of communication. The committee will realize that, as I have said before, the number of men in the division itself, that is to say, what we regard as the division proper, is augmented and has to be augmented and supplemented very considerably by men on lines of communication, for working with the corps and for working with the army.
We emerge, then, with two corps. It was stated by the Prime Minister that one of the two corps would consist of three infantry divisions and the other corps of two armoured divisions. That may or may not be the composition of those corps. We want to have them perfectly flexible, and it may be that the composition of the corps will change from time to time, depending upon whether or not it may be desirable to use an armoured division with an infantry division, or an armoured division with two infantry divisions, or otherwise as the case may be. Those two corps will compose the Canadian army, which will have an army headquarters and will be a complete organization, what I described before as a hard-hitting, fast-moving fighting force ready to take on any job which may present itself. That does not mean by any means that this army has to fight as a unit. I have said before, and I repeat, that those with whom we are associated understand full well
__and I know this personally because I have
made it clear to them myself-that the Canadian army and the Canadian troops are, the Prime Minister said the other day, for the purpose of serving the common cause to the very best advantage, that they are prepared to serve in whatever theatre and in whatever way may be considered best, having regard to the task which has to be done.
That is our overseas programme. That will require, as I anticipate, something like 100,000 men by the end of the ensuing fiscal year. Of those, roughly 25,000 will be for new units, that is to say, for those additional corps and army units, and something like 75,000 for reinforcements.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes, or intended for
overseas.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
