maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I did not get that clearly. Did the minister say there would be a total of 175,000 go overseas this year?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. I have in mind that the army will have something like 175,000, but it all depends upon casualties, as my hon. friend knows.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Did you mean that there were 175,000 to be raised for overseas this year?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No. I said 100,000, of which 25,000, roughly, were for new units, and 75,000 for reinforcements. That is our programme.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Will they be ready by the end of the year?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would think so, yes- earlier than that. That is our programme for overseas, as we see it at the present time. I intimated, in addition, that we had certain plans in Canada. Certain special dispositions had been made, due to the worsening of the situation following Pearl Harbour. These dispositions had been made particularly on the east and west coasts.
I need hardly say one of the most important items of those dispositions was the formation of anti-aircraft batteries-that is, so far as the army is concerned. That has been followed up. Along with that, as the Prime Minister said yesterday, has gone the formation of about a dozen new infantry battalions, and a certain number of additional artillery batteries and other arms of the service.
In addition to that, there has been authorization for an organization of reserve brigade groups. That is to say, reserve
War Appropriation

battalions across Canada have been authorized in each district to form into reserve brigades, and permanent staffs have been provided for those brigades, in order that they may have training, and be in a position to assist in connection with the defence of Canada, should the need arise.
In addition to that, there have been arrangements made for the organization of men in training centres into a special formation for use in emergency conditions.
All those are, of course, in addition to the fourth division, which is now in Canada; in addition to the three brigade groups of the sixth division, which is in Canada; and in addition to the coast defence artillery units, and their supplementary services, which are on both coasts.
That would have been quite a comprehensive programme. Then, in addition to that- it was not in the Prime Minister's announcement-I should point out to the committee that we have authorized the completion of the sixth division as a self-contained formation, by providing divisional troops and divisional headquarters which, along with the three brigade groups of the sixth division, which have been mobilized for some time, will form a complete sixth division.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Does that include artillery?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Artillery, engineers and all units of other services. The commanding officer of the sixth division will be, I expect, named very shortly.
Then, as the Prime Minister said, we have authorized the mobilization of the seventh division. That is to say, it will be the mobilization of a complete seventh division, which means the infantry battalions, plus all services-artillery, engineers, signals, army service corps, medical corps, and so on-a complete division.
That division will be mobilized and composed of units which are already in being by forming them into brigades, and putting alongside them in brigade groups the various services required. Headquarters will be provided as well.
Following that will be the 'mobilization of -he eighth division, which will also be formed,
I anticipate, from units which have already been mobilized-or some which have been mobilized very recently, and probably with the addition of some to be mobilized. Hon. members will understand that that does not mean that the formation of the seventh and eighth divisions simply means the conversion into divisions of battalions which up to this time have been individual battalions. That will be so, but battalions will have to be 
organized to take the place of those battalions which will go into these two divisions. That is to say, we are adding to our strength in Canada to the extent of these divisions.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But not attested.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Do you call them active forces?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am calling them that. Each of these units will have some in them who are attested. A very large proportion will be men who have been called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is true of the sixth division also.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The sixth division was very much less. I would1 say probably 20 per cent, or less, are under the National Resources Mobilization Act at the present time.

speechtext: Is it the intention to take any of the present second battalions, and make them a part of the seventh and eighth divisions?

But, answering the hon. member for Yale, do not let anyone think there will not be plenty of second battalions still in existence. I am answering the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, too. That is the programme, very roughly, for the year. In that connection I do not believe I have anything more to say at this time. speechtext:

44S61-108
called up. This "Order of Battle" has not been given out, and perhaps hon. members will note that it is not being given in the Canada Gazette. If my hon. friend wants to know about any particular unit, I can give him the information.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Will the minister explain
about the reserve army? Figures have been given from time to time showing that there are about 140,000 men in the reserve army, and a return brought down in this house shows that about 62,000 of these are men who were called up for thirty days' training under the National Resources Mobilization Act and then returned to their homes after completing their training. The only connection they have with the army is that their names appear on the nominal rolls of the reserve units to which they have been posted. In other words, they have not been taking any training with the reserve units at all and are really no longer in the army; yet they are always shown as part of the reserve army. This would appear to make the strength of that reserve army quite a lot larger than it really should be. It really amounts to a paper strength. Furthermore, there was a return No. 1241 brought down on March 23 which includes a copy of a letter from the acting deputy minister for the army to the under-secretary of state, which contains this paragraph:
No information is available concerning the number of enlistments among personnel who were called for 30 days' training and who have not yet been recalled for further training.
In other words, of these 62,000 men we do not know how many have enlisted for active service. They may be in the active army, the navy or the air force; they certainly are no longer in the reserve army. I think these points should be cleared up by the minister.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend is perfectly right when he says that when men enlist in the active forces, they are not available as part of the reserve army.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But they still appear as part.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I heard what my hon.
friend said. I understand about that. To that extent I think the figures are incorrect, but it does not mean that we have lost those men. It means that they have become more useful than if they W'ere still in the reserve army-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I maintain-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Will my hon, friend just
permit me to finish the sentence? It means, of course, that they are being counted in the reserve army and in the active army too. I

War Appropriation

think my hon. friend is perfectly right in his criticism. I know of no way that that could be corrected except to take a percentage.
My hon. friend is not quite correct in his reference to paper strength. These men have had thirty days of intensive training. Knowing what I do of the training of the reserve army, I would think that really qualifies them to be members of the reserve army. I quite understand that they do not go to the armouries, but they are there and available for the reserve army and therefore I think they might properly be counted. My hon. friend is only repeating what he said in the house the other day. He referred to the reserve army and much to my surprise indicated that he thought the reserve army should be called up compulsorily for training.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I said if they could not be obtained in any other way.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is how I would have expected my hon. friend to put it, rather than the way I put it. It is the easiest thing in the world for the Department of National Defence to make a requisition to the Department of National War Services for them to ask so many men to report for training. The reserve army is a citizen's army, organized and mobilized for the primary purpose of defending the homes of the people who are in them and their communities.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then these 60,000 should not be counted in the reserve army.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I say that that is not the idea of the reserve army. It is pointed out by my officers that the suggestion which my hon. friend makes that they should be called up for compulsory service is a complete negation of our whole idea of the reserve army. But I say to him that if it is necessary in this time of stress to call on our citizens compulsorily to defend their communities, then it will have to be done. But I do feel that we ought to give these citizens a proper opportunity to enlist in that reserve army and to do their share with respect to the defence of their homes and the communities in which they live. The reserve army essentially is one which lives and thrives on the patriotic fervour and self-denial of the men who are in it, men who are willing to give up something for the sake of assisting in the defence of their country; men who are willing to stay after hours; men who are willing to take extra classes; men who are willing to make the best use of little equipment perhaps; men who are willing to wait for their turn on a
iMr. Ralston.]
piece of equipment in order that they may fit themselves. I feel just as strongly as my hon. friend, perhaps a little stronger, with regard to calling men up compulsorily, but I do feel that we should not do that until we have made dead sure that the citizens in these communities understand what their responsibilities are and have had an opportunity to fulfil them.
It is obvious that the citizens are not coming into the ranks of the reserve army as we would like them to. There are only two ways to get them, voluntarily or by calling them up. There is a place for the reserve army in our organization. Men below 19 years of age or from 35 to 50 years are taken into the reserve army. Recognition is given to the fact that these are men who probably are not in a position, because of age, family responsibility, or business responsibilities, to take their part in the active army. We have just decided to do one thing more in this respect, that is to lower the age limit from 35 to 30 years in the case of married men. We are doing this in the hope that we will get more men into the reserve army. I say to my hon. friend and to the committee that I am perfectly ready to consider the calling up of men compulsorily for the reserve army if that is the only way in which they can be brought in. I hope that will not be so because I think it would defeat the spirit which is behind the reserve army and which has done so much to build up the active battalions we have. The whole Canadian army has been built up on the reserve army. The units which are overseas were reserve army units which were mobilized. This is entirely different from the situation in the last war. As I say, the whole army is built up on the organization, the esprit de corps, of the units of the reserve army.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Does the minister not think that the best way to build up the reserve army would be for the government to decide how many men it wants and then make an appeal to the people of Canada for that number to enlist? These men have had all kinds of discouragements, and I am not surprised at all that there has been great trouble in keeping these units up to strength. The position now, it is quite evident, is that there are only about 80,000 men in the reserve, the difference between that number and 140,000 being made up of these thirty-day trainees, and they by the way are not volunteers, so they do not fit in with the minister's description of the purposes of the reserve army. It does seem to me that if the ministry

War Appropriation
would announce how large a reserve they are going to have-100,000 or 200,000 or whatever the number may be-and then go out and appeal for these men, they would have no trouble in getting them.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am not going to let
my hon. friend or any other member of this house suggest that the government should necessarily set a target for the total reserve army. My hon. friend knows perfectly well the reserve units in a particular community. Their officers know the number of men they want and all you have to do is to ask them. It is the community that primarily has to do with the reserve units. We have reserve brigade groups right across this dominion. We have reserve units in each district, and I ask hon. members to assist in encouraging a community spirit and in asking men to go into the reserve airmy. If the emergency exists which has been pointed out in this house and in the country, I cannot conceive of men not responding if the matter is properly put to them, not only by the government, but by people in their own community.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If all the reserve units were brought up to strength, what would the total strength of the reserve army be?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I cannot tell my hon.
friend without knowing the number of the reserve units.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What is the approximate
strength of the reserve army now, after subtracting the number of thirty-day trainees?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been
given the figures. I have not the strength returns, but if there are 140,000 on the reserve army and 60,000 of supernumeraries, that makes 80,000.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I understand that 90,000 men
were called for thirty days' training.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But a good many of them have been called up and are on service now. That number is going down all the time as men are called up for four months' training and going into active service. That number is getting less and less. Do I make myself clear?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If the minister cannot say how many men will be required to complete all the reserve units, surely he can tell the committee how many men will be required to bring up to strength all the reserve units which have been ordered brigaded.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
For one reserve brigade, about 3,000 men. Multiply that by eleven districts; eleven times 3,000 would make it 33,000.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is it the intention of the department to have one brigade in each military division, or will all the reserve force units be brigaded in time?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The plan has not been to brigade all the reserve force units. The brigade plan was for a special purpose at a particular time. The reserves have never been brigaded, with an active full-time brigade staff. They have been in their regular brigades in their particular locality, but all on a part-time basis. For operational purposes administration and training staff have been provided for one brigade in each of the districts. That does not mean that the other reserve units are not operating as they always have been.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: From what medical categories are the reserve army drawn?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think it goes down as low as "C", but I cannot tell my hon. friend to-night. My hon. friend the member for Vancouver South asked me a question with regard to the reserve army and with regard to strength, and that gave me an opportunity to give the committee what I had made a note of, namely my hon. friend's suggestion that the reserve army should be completed by the calling up of men for service under the National Resources Mobilization Act. May I say to him that I thoroughly agree with some of the things that have been said. The reserve army has had a good deal of discouragement. Their functions have been changed twice that I know of, having regard to the particular situation in which we found ourselves. The reserve army units at first had the expectation of being mobilized, and each one of them held on to the men in their particular ranks as active service men. They did not want them to go as reinforcements because they entertained the hope that they would be mobilized for active service. That hope faded in a great many cases; some of the active service men went to other units from the locality or elsewhere, and that caused discouragement. The suggestion was made and followed of setting up an organization whereby they were asked to keep a certain percentage of their personnel in the active service category, A category men, so that they could furnish reinforcements and at the same time carry on reserve units proper. Then that was reviewed. Representations were made to the department by some of the reserve units themselves. They felt that the reserve units were in competition with the active service units in the matter of recruiting, and they felt that the age limit should be changed so that men between 19 and 35 years
War Appropriation

of age would not enlist in the reserve units. That age limit has been in force now for some little time. As I have indicated, an order is just going out now that the age limit will be changed for married men from 35 to 30.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is the situation about the single man from 30 to 35 who cannot enter the reserve army and cannot be called up? Would the minister tell us about that?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What does my hon. friend mean by "tell us about that"?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What is to become of that particular class?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I suppose they could enlist.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They cannot be called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: These men can enlist. Under the National Resources Mobilization Act, all one has to do to call them up is to issue a proclamation increasing the age limit. That has not been done, but a proclamation can be issued, and probably might be in the very near future, so that these men could be called up. In the meantime, they can enlist in the active service.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Why should there be that gap? The Prime Minister announced that the government was only going to call men up to thirty years of age, from twenty-one to thirty, and they are to be chosen by lot. Why that gap between thirty and thirty-five? You are allowing the married men from thirty to thirty-five in the reserve, but not the single men.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The government did not announce that they would not take men over thirty but that they would take any man up to thirty. They may announce at any time that they will take any man from thirty to thirty-five. I think it is perhaps a pretty good policy that single men from thirty to thirty-five should be encouraged to enlist. It has been represented by officers commanding units that there are cases in which a man does not realize his duty to enlist if he is in a reserve unit. The situation is that there is a place for that man to serve. He has not been called up at the present time, but he may be called up. I do not see any harm being done to the national interest or to the army by what my hon. friend calls that gap, which is really not a gap at all.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
A man from thirty to thirty-five is supposed to enlist in the active service

force, but a man from twenty-one to thirty is called up for home service. Why are they not all treated in the same way?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would say that the man from twenty-one to thirty has the same opportunity to enlist in the active service forces. The man from twenty-one to thirty has two opportunities: he is liable to be called up, and his alternative is to enlist in the active service forces. The man from thirty to thirty-five is not liable to be called up as the proclamation stands at present. But he does have the opportunity, or liability, or obligation, or whatever he may want to call it, to enlist from thirty to thirty-five. If any preference were given, it was given to the man from thirty to thirty-five.
Progress reported.
